Johann Sebastian Bach (1685~1750)

Widely recognized as a prolific composer of the late-Baroque era, Johann Sebastian Bach wrote many of the most well-known Baroque and Classical pieces of all time. His musically domineering presence from centuries ago left deep footprints that are visible even today. Although largely uncelebrated during his lifetime, his vast repertoire is widely celebrated and studied. Examining Bach’s life through the pieces composed during his time is essential to understanding the enigma that he was. 

Early Childhood

Like many great composers, Johann Sebastian Bach was raised in a religious musical family. He was the youngest of seven siblings, many of whom pursued music as a full-time profession, Bach being no exception. He was taught to play the violin and harpsichord by his father, Johann Ambrosius, and later on was shown by his uncle how to play the organ, which he extensively studied. The organ was the core of his lifelong passion, and his love for it was evident even when he was young. 
Despite being a successful and respectable musician later in his life, Bach’s childhood was marked with sadness and misfortune. When Bach was ten years old, his mother and father died during the years 1694 and 1695, respectively. Bach’s life suffered drastic changes from this point forward, one of which included moving in with his brother, Johann Christoph, who assisted in the advancement of Bach’s musical career. 
One of the earliest unverified pieces accredited to Bach is “Fugue in E minor”. This was allegedly composed in 1707, when Bach was to have been ten or fifteen years old. The reason why it is classified as “unverified” is partly because of the lack of conservation of music during his time. Many experts claim that this fugue is his earliest musical work, while others argue that it isn’t his work due to the lack of a signature and the stylistic difference between his verified work and the fugue. A plethora of other works also suffered the same unfortunate fate, as many manuscripts and records were recovered, but none were able to be determined for certain whether it was his work. 

Young Adulthood 
Aus der Tiefen rufe ich, Herr, zu dir, BWV 131

Like many things in musical history, the first official piece of a composer is heavily disputed and dissected among experts. Although there are many sources of conflicting information, claiming some compositions were produced before others, many experts agree that the first proved composition of Johann Sebastian Bach is a cantata named “Aus de Tiefen rufe ich, Herr, zu dir,” which in English means, “From the Depths, I call, Lord”. The church cantata was written around 1707, which was around the time Bach was working as an organist in Arnstadt at the age of twenty-two. Being a religious man, and with the addition of his new church profession, Bach was likely influenced by his religious upbringing to compose this piece, which is further indicated by the title of his work, which is associated with the Christian religion. 
Bach obtained his job as an organist after finishing school, starting first as a court musician. He quickly was able to ascend to prestigious positions. During this era of his life, he was still developing his compositional characteristics and voice. The cantata reflects his growing skill in artistic ability. Even at this stage in his life, Bach was not known for being flashy or overly ostentatious, but he built a deceivingly effortless melody based on technicality, and pinpoint precision when utilizing counterpoint. Counterpoint refers to the composer’s ability to weave two or more melodies. To create an effective and beautiful polyphonic texture, the composer needs to create two melodies that can sustain themselves in terms of rhythm while maintaining harmony. Even while moving and switching professions, this is an aspect that Bach is well known for and considered one of the masters of counterpoint, which is evident even in his earlier works, such as  Aus der Tiefen rufe ich, Herr, zu dir.

Weimar and Imprisonment 
Toccata and Fugue in F major (BMV 540) 

During the middle of Bach’s career, he expanded from his organ-focused works to a much wider instrumental and vocal palette. In Arnstadt and Munchhausen, where he lived for nearly a decade, his repertoire consisted mainly of organ and harpsichord pieces, like the Prelude and Fugue in G minor. This was very evident within his works when he lived in Weimar, where he wrote Toccata and Fugue in F major, described as powerful and dramatic, a notable work of his.  
Bach had been commissioned by the Duke of Weimar to write a cantata every month, and he wrote thirty in total during his stay. However, like the majority of his career, Bach moved frequently depending on the jobs that he had. Around this time, when he had accepted the position as a court member for Prince Leopold, he was imprisoned by the duke for accepting his new position at Prince Leopold’s court before being permitted to do so. 

The Slow Transition 
Chaconne, Partita No.2 BMV 1004 

Eventually, Bach was released, and he moved to Köthen to work for the prince. This marked the slow shift away from the organ and more towards the instrumental genre. This was likely because Prince Leopold was more fond of secular music rather than the religious style cantatas that Bach had been accustomed to writing for Duke Wilhelm Ernst of Weimar. As he slowly moved away stylistically from religion, the frequency with which he produced pieces for the organ diminished. The organ, at the time, was heavily affiliated with the Christian religion. It is because of the prince’s preference for secular music that Bach was encouraged to move away from the organ. 
This was the catalyst that allowed Bach to expand into the secular genre, producing many of what are considered his best works, like the Brandenburg Orchestral Concertos. The Brandenburg Concertos were composed in six, and gifted to the Margrave of Brandenburg, in an attempt to obtain a position in his court. But these concertos were ignored, and unfortunately were never played during Bach’s lifetime, being filed for nearly a century before being recovered. 
Other notable works of his include the Sonatas and Partitas for Solo Violin. His set of sonatas and partitas for the violin is a rite of passage for budding violinists, as it is very technique-heavy and in turn hones in on the student’s musical maturity. Unlike many of Bach’s works, which were commissioned or written because of his profession, Bach wrote the Sonatas and Partitas for Solo Violin of his own volition, although his reasons for doing so are not definitively known. 
One of the most famous parts of his Sonatas and Partitas is the Chaconne in Partita No.2. Described as heavy and dark, it was apparently written after the premature death of his first wife and mother to seven children, hence the emotional theme. It is said that she died while Bach was on a trip to Carlsbad and was told of her passing long after she died. Professor Helga Thoene, a German musicologist,  theorized that the partita was dedicated to Maria Barbara as a memorial, but whether this is true is heavily debated by musical historians. 
Regardless of Bach’s intentions behind writing the Sonatas and Partitas, many believe this era of Bach’s life solidified his career and identity, allowing him to flourish creatively. 

Golden and Middle Age 
Mass in B Minor 

Despite his growing reputation and respect within the musical community, Bach was regarded as a family man, fathering nearly twenty children between two wives. With his first wife, Maria Barbara, he fathered seven children, only four reaching adulthood. After the death of his first wife, he met 20-year-old Anna Magdalena during the year 1721, when she was working as a singer while he worked as a music director. In their marriage, the couple conceived thirteen children, six of whom reached adulthood. Four out of ten adult children became composers like their father, but they were never able to reach the level of fame that their father had. 
Despite his middle age being defined by recurrent loss of loved ones, he advanced professionally and musically, approaching his absolute peak. His peak was reached after he moved to Leipzig after resigning from his position in Prince Leopold’s court. He left his position because of the diminishment of the orchestra due to the worsening financial status of the prince. 
Although Bach tended to move around in the pursuit of a better job, he stayed in Leipzig for the remainder of his life, which was nearly three decades. During this period, he composed a cantata a week for his job as a music director. This was considered his musical prime when he produced his best works, such as Mass in B minor, nearly two hours long, which has a section titled “Crucifixus”, referencing the crucification of Jesus Christ. Despite being a devout Lutheran, he wrote a mass that aligned with Catholic-style music. The piece has a heavy theological theme, and many of the sections are titled after Christian religious events. The piece was apparently written between 1748 and 1749, as Bach slowly reached the end of his life. The Mass in B minor is a combination of multiple musical styles and his Lutheran faith, and it is no wonder that it is regarded as his “Magnum Opus,” which refers to the best work of a composer. 

Near the End 
The Art of Fugue- Contrapunctus No.14 

As Bach inched near the end of his life, he was afflicted by numerous illnesses and diseases. According to the National Library of Medicine, they claimed that Bach lived an unhealthy lifestyle, one that consisted of consuming an excessive amount of alcohol and tobacco. Other experts of the same source claim that Bach may have had diabetes. 
In short, Bach had a plethora of medical afflictions, and the attempted treatment of one inadvertently caused his death. According to an article published on the site, Oxford Bach Soloists, during the early 1750s, Bach’s vision apparently became abhorrent due to cataracts. While not life-threatening, it interfered with his ability to compose and live normally. For this reason, he sought the medical assistance of a controversial eye doctor named John Taylor, who claimed to be able to restore or at least improve Bach’s sight. However, Taylor had an unsteady reputation, allegedly blinding a great number of patients because of the results of his failed procedures. 
Nevertheless, Bach underwent two procedures to improve his eyesight before becoming permanently blind. Many historians believe that this series of surgeries was a last resort to restore his vision. As a consequence of the injuries sustained during the second corrective operation, he was left unable to conduct or compose. Four months after the procedure, due to the immense stress on his body, and his already deteriorating health, revered composer Johann Sebastian Bach passed away from a stroke on July 28th of the year 1750. However, prior to Bach’s death, he had been writing his last piece, called the Unfinished Fugue, Contrapunctus 14. 
This fugue is one of the most famous works of Bach because the piece ended abruptly due to Bach’s death and was never completed. Additionally, next to the final note, an F natural on the stained, yellowed paper, is a small note written by one of his sons, stating that the composer Bach had passed away before completing the work. Although it is possible that Bach indeed finished the fugue and that the final manuscript was never recovered, there is no existing evidence supporting that theory. 
Regardless of whether the Unfinished Fugue was completed, it is considered a masterpiece as it encapsulates Bach’s musical genius, his near-perfect use of polyphony, and his mastery in writing fugues. It demonstrates how although the health and wellness of Bach were rapidly degenerating, his passion for music never diminished. 

Conclusion 

Overall, through the lens of historical books, the legacy of Johann Sebastian Bach has been blurred and muddled. The glorification of the art that he created often dismissed the hardship of producing great works of art. His fugues and sonatas are studied by millions of music students, and for good reason. His passion and adoration for his craft transcend time, with his emotions acting as a foundation to his greatest work. Despite the suffering he faced, such as the loss of his children, his first wife, and his eyesight, Bach created beauty that needed neither words nor colors.

Classical music presents itself as a realm of depth, rigor, and artistic seriousness, yet the surrounding culture often feels cold rather than inviting. Musical snobs rarely announce themselves openly. Instead, they communicate exclusion through small gestures that carry unusual weight. A corrected pronunciation delivered with a slight smirk, a remark implying someone’s “basic” taste, or a loud silence after an enthusiastic but imperfect comment can shape a newcomer’s entire perception of the field. These interactions may seem minor to insiders, but to the person receiving them, they reveal the unwritten rules of belonging.

The roots of this atmosphere run deep. Classical music was supported for centuries by courts, religious institutions, and wealthy patronage, and portions of that heritage linger in the culture. People who were raised around lessons, ensembles, and academic music programs assumed this education as the norm. They don’t notice how often they reference theory vocabulary or composer pedigrees, because these details feel ordinary to them. But someone stepping into the field without that foundation can feel as if they are arriving in a room where every conversation assumes knowledge they were never given.

This tension intensifies inside elite conservatories. Students in these institutions receive inspiring and rigorous training, but the culture can also breed insecurity, competition, and status anxiety. Some students use their technical command as a badge of superiority, treating anyone outside their circle as musically uninformed. Talent is measured in awards, accolades, and orchestral seating, as students vie for first place. Others internalize the pressure and begin believing that worth is measured by repertoire difficulty, faculty endorsements, and acceptance into prestigious programs. When this outlook colors how they talk to others, it makes the field seem closed to anyone who didn’t pass through that exclusive educational environment.

What makes this gatekeeping especially ironic is that many revered composers actively resisted narrow ideas about their art. Beethoven broke structures with relentless confidence. Mozart wrote for public spaces and popular gatherings that welcomed lively energy. Newer composers continue to push boundaries through experimental harmony, unconventional instrumentation, and collaborations that extend far beyond traditional settings. The history of the genre thrives on reinvention, yet parts of the community behave as though strict uniformity protects it.

Moving classical music toward greater openness doesn’t mean erasing tradition. It means rethinking how knowledge is shared and how curiosity is treated. Teachers should welcome questions that seem simple. Performers can greet new audiences with warmth, not silence. Conservatory students can speak about technique without implying that mastery and elite schooling guarantee superiority. Listeners at concerts can respond to enthusiasm with patience instead of judgment. None of this diminishes the music’s complexity. It simply enlarges the space where people can enter.

When classical music stops guarding itself so intensely, it becomes easier for listeners to approach it without fear of embarrassment. The genre only gains value when people feel invited to experience it rather than evaluated while doing so. Obliterating habits of snobbery helps restore the art’s original power, reestablishing it as music that reaches people because it is expressive, human, and open to anyone willing to listen.

Sampling is one of those topics that everyone seems to have a strong opinion on. Some see it as creative and essential, while others view it as lazy or even unethical. Much of this tension resurfaced recently when a social media post highlighting Middle Eastern music sampled by hip-hop artists trended online. What began as a celebration of musical connection quickly turned into a broader argument about originality, legality, and artistic integrity. 

At its core, sampling is simply the use of pre-recorded sound within a new piece of music. Like any artistic tool, it can be used carelessly or with intention. When done well, sampling is not a shortcut but a form of expression that reshapes existing sounds into something new. Entire genres, especially hip-hop and electronic music, are built on this practice. Albums such as Endtroducing….., Madvillainy, and To Pimp A Butterfly are often praised for their innovation, yet they would not exist without sampling. Producers like J Dilla, Madlib, Kanye West, RZA, Q-Tip, and DJ Shadow used fragments of older recordings to create music that feels timeless and deeply personal.

Academic research supports the idea that sampling is less about copying and more about dialogue. In The Sampling Continuum: Musical Aesthetics and Ethics in the Age of Digital Production (Behr, 2017), it is argued that musicians often hold onto romantic ideas of originality, even though their creative practices depend heavily on past work. Influence and acquisition frequently overlap, and artists themselves recognize that the boundary between the two is unclear. Sampling, then, is often rooted in respect and admiration for earlier music rather than exploitation.

The ethical debate becomes more complicated when industry power dynamics are considered. Copyright laws are meant to protect artists, but they often favor major labels and rights holders. Independent musicians rarely have the financial or legal support needed to clear samples, even when their work is transformative. For some, accusations of unauthorized sampling can be financially devastating. This reality has led to the discouragement of publicly identifying samples, sometimes referred to as “sample snitching,” because drawing attention to them can create serious consequences for smaller artists.

Questions of plagiarism in music are rarely straightforward. Cases like the long-running debate over whether Led Zeppelin’s “Stairway to Heaven” borrowed from Spirit’s “Taurus” show how subjective these judgments can be. Musical ideas repeat across history, whether intentionally or not. Sampling differs in that it often openly acknowledges its sources, especially in hip-hop, where older and sometimes obscure recordings are reintroduced to new audiences through reinterpretation.

Ultimately, sampling connects generations and cultures while pushing music forward. While ethical and legal concerns should not be ignored, dismissing sampling outright ignores its artistic value and cultural impact. Music has always evolved through borrowing, influence, and reinvention. Sampling is simply one of the clearest expressions of that tradition.

Music has become so integrated into social media that many of the songs we now hear on the radio, in stores, and at gatherings actually gained popularity by first going viral online. In fact, 84 percent of hit songs on Billboard’s Global 200 first went viral on TikTok in 2024. With the recent rise of social media, hit songs can reach billions of users; thus, social media algorithms have changed the way music becomes popular.

Often, songs can go viral when they are associated with a viral trend. For example, “Say So” by Doja Cat went viral on TikTok in 2020 for its addictively catchy dance. The song naturally gained popularity as millions of users learned the dance, with its official music video even featuring the TikTok dance. 

Additionally, algorithms promote content based solely on user engagement, leveling the playing field for small artists. Take PinkPantheress, who grew from a small, unnoticed artist to a Grammy nominee within five years. She began posting clips of her music on SoundCloud, but wasn’t widely discovered until 2021 on TikTok. Her music went viral for its unique vocals, 2000s nostalgia, and danceable beats. The authenticity of her style was refreshing to listeners, as it did not conform to the typical pop song formula. Her audience quickly expanded beyond social media as she performed on stages around the world. In 2024, she was even named Billboard’s Woman Producer of the Year, proving the algorithm to be a powerful tool for emerging artists by highlighting and promoting their talent.

Because short-form video algorithms promote content that can quickly make a flashy impression, musical artists now work within a much shorter time frame to capture listeners’ attention. They have adapted by creating immediate hooks in their songs: statistically, the time it takes for vocals to begin in viral tracks dropped by 78% from 1986 to 2015. Artists may also incorporate steady, danceable rhythms, repetitive phrases, and catchy lyrics to increase their chances of going viral.

However, what happens when music-making becomes algorithmic? Virality has complicated things for artists. In an interview with The Forty-Five, Grammy-winning rapper Doechii discusses how considering how to attract popularity on social media could take away from the art of creativity in music production: “I don’t want hip-hop or art to get distracted and lost in trying to make music for a computer.” Indeed, songs created to fit a formula can sound repetitive and lack originality, such as “abcdefu” by Gayle, which listeners criticized for sounding “manufactured” to feed into the algorithm. 

Lastly, while social media is a powerful way to boost a song’s popularity, a work’s reputation can also be tarnished by being called a TikTok song. “If it feels too much like a TikTok song, nobody thinks that’s cool,” Doechii states. Songs that are “overhyped” on social media due to user engagement, not to a characteristic of the song or musical artist, are generally weaker and lack originality. Thus, it is unfortunate for artists who work hard to produce a new hit, only for it to be stigmatized by a 15-second clip. 

Whether we like it or not, the overwhelming power of social media algorithms has fundamentally changed how music is discovered. While it is a powerful aid to music discovery, it can also be a burden for artists whose balance between individuality and conformity is exacerbated. In reality, social media has become deeply embedded in our daily lives and culture, so musical artists must adapt to it.

Artificial intelligence has existed for many years, but it has only recently has it become a major influence on people’s lives. Now, rather than being just a background tool in technology, it has entered the foreground of music creation. Medium's “The Future of Music: How Artificial Intelligence Is Shaping the Industry” by Christian Mark and Substream Magazine’s “AI and Its Influence on Music Creation: The Future of Sound” reveal that AI is transforming music in ways that expand creative possibilities for both artists and listeners. However, this prospect also raises tough questions about authenticity, ownership, and the role of human artists. 

The idea that AI will not replace human musicians but rather act as a collaborator in music production is emphasized by both articles. As Substream notes, AI “acts as a collaborative tool that helps musicians explore new ideas.” AI can generate melodies or harmonies that help inspire many artists and give them a starting point to work with. Mark remarks that it provides opportunities for bedroom producers and non-musicians to experiment without needing years of experience or expensive studios.

One of AI’s most immediate impacts lies in its efficiency. According to Substream, AI tools are already simplifying “tasks such as beat-making, sound design, and audio engineering,” allowing creators to focus on expression rather than technical barriers. For listeners, AI can provide individualized experiences. Streaming platforms already recommend tracks, but the future could go much further into it. Imagine playlists that adapt to your mood in real time, or music that shifts in tempo and tone to match your heart rate. This kind of personalized music may redefine the relationship between artist and audience.

Despite these benefits, both articles stress the serious challenges that come with it. One major challenge for them is copyright. If AI composes an entire piece of music, the question of who truly owns it, the developer, the user, or the AI system itself, is left for the listeners. Mark warns that reliance on AI creates the risk of uncredited borrowing, raising questions of fairness and originality.

There is also the concern that AI could flatten creativity because overreliance on machine-generated outputs may result in “a homogenized sound that lacks the unique touch of human artists,” Mark cautions. Artists risk losing their authenticity if they use AI as a shortcut instead of a creative tool. While the future of music might be different from what we know, it's certainly becoming more collaborative and creative!

Rhythm is essential to all music, and its effects on the mind and body have been known and studied. Beginning with ancient rituals and continuing through modern music therapy, rhythm has played an important role in culture and healing. Rhythm has a profound connection with physical and psychological states, stemming from our biological rhythm and bodily responses to stimuli. Music therapy, the focus of Solis and Luna Arts and a growing field of practice, utilizes the power of rhythm in music to promote people’s well-being. 

The human body is essentially rhythmic. Many of the processes your body carries out are governed by rhythms, such as your heartbeat, breathing, and circadian rhythm. These biological functions provide a foundation for how external stimuli, like music, can influence your internal state. When we listen to music, especially those with a steady rhythm, our bodies will synchronize with it. This event, known as entrainment, occurs when your body’s internal rhythm matches the external. For instance, the heart rate will speed up or slow down depending on the beat of the music you listen to. As a result, people will typically work out to upbeat or fast-paced music.

One of the most well-recorded effects of rhythm on the human body is its ability to prompt relaxation. Slow and steady rhythms are often used in music therapy to induce a state of calm and reduce anxiety. This effect is largely due to the heart and breathing rates matching the slow beat. As the body synchronizes, the parasympathetic nervous system is activated, producing a relaxation response. This response is indicated by a slowed heart rate and muscle relaxation, creating a sense of peace. With this, rhythm can be used for relaxation or even energization, depending on what you want your outcome to be. In music therapy, any instrument can be used to help patients achieve a desired state. All instruments can create rhythmic patterns that can be effective for individuals dealing with stress, anxiety, or insomnia. By helping others transition into a relaxed state, rhythm can improve sleep quality and reduce symptoms of pain.

Rhythm is not only beneficial to the physical self but also has a powerful impact on cognitive function and attention. Research in music therapy has shown that rhythmic stimuli enhance concentration and improve performance. It has also been shown to be useful for people suffering from brain illnesses like stroke, traumatic brain injury, or Parkinson's disease. All of this is linked to rhythm, which engages multiple areas of the brain, including those responsible for coordination, timing, and attention. For example, rhythmic auditory stimulation, a music therapy technique, uses rhythmic cues to enhance motor function and walking ability in patients with movement issues. On the topic of motor function, patients with Parkinson’s disease also benefit from rhythmic cueing, which helps them synchronize their movements with the beat and helps them focus. In the realm of cognitive rehabilitation, rhythm-based techniques have been used to improve focus and memory in people with brain injuries. The structure of rhythm helps organize thoughts and memories, making it easier for people to concentrate. 

The emotional effects of rhythm are another benefit to the mind. Since it has the ability to evoke and regulate emotion, it has become a valuable tool in music therapy for emotional processing. Different patterns trigger different responses; using the example from earlier, fast rhythms evoke excitement or joy, while slow can evoke calm or sadness. In therapy, it is often used to help patients process and express emotions that may be difficult to articulate. For patients with anxiety or depression, engaging with music can create a sense of stability. The repetitive nature can help soothe the mind and help with their emotions.

In conclusion, rhythm is a powerful force that influences the mind and body in profound ways. It plays a central role in music therapy by promoting relaxation, enhancing cognitive function, and helping with emotions. By utilizing the body's innate ability to synchronize with rhythms, we can help individuals achieve a wide range of therapeutic goals. The appeal of rhythm, combined with its ability to engage the mind and body, makes it an indispensable tool for music therapy.

Art is typically done to relax and express creative energy. However, the particular benefits of artistic expression go deeper than simply relaxation and enjoyment. Studies suggest that art therapy can be very valuable in treating depression, anxiety, PTSD, and even a number of phobias. It is a way to process complex feelings and express your emotions without the hassle of “finding the right words”.

What Exactly Is Art Therapy?

Art therapy, defined in the simplest way, is an application of the visual arts in a therapeutic context. However, keep in mind, a therapist is not necessary in order to experience the therapeutic benefits of artistic expression. There are many different forms of expression you can try from the comfort of your home such as art journaling, sketching, painting, creating collages, clay sculpting, etc. It doesn’t matter what media you choose. The only thing that matters is your enjoyment!

However, working with a licensed therapist also has its advantages. A professional can tailor each activity to your personal preference. If the activities are done in a group, they are a great method for developing healthy connections with other people. This comes in handy for people fighting depression. The most important thing is that you should try art therapy only if you want it. Expressing yourself through art requires a level of vulnerability, so if you still don’t feel ready, that is okay.

Why Should You Try It

Art therapy is a service that improves the lives of individuals and communities through active art-making, creative process and human experience. Art therapy, with a professional art therapist, supports personal and relational treatment goals as well as community concerns.
Honoring individuals’ personal values and beliefs, art therapists work along people who are struggling with medical and/or mental health disorders. Individuals are typically seeking emotional, creative and spiritual growth.

Art therapy engages the mind and body in ways that are different from language alone. Visual and symbolic expression shines light on experience and inspired individual, communal and societal transformation.

Songwriting is becoming an increasingly meaningful tool in music therapy because it helps people express emotions, build confidence, and connect with others in a creative way. Music therapist Catherine Backus, MT-BC, explains that one of her main goals is to make music creation feel accessible to anyone, no matter their musical background or past struggles. She shares that songwriting helped her handle her own feelings when she was younger, and she now uses that same process to support her clients.

Research shows that songwriting can strengthen group relationships, encourage healthy emotional expression, improve self-esteem, and help people understand their own needs and those of others (Backus, 2018). Songs can hold emotional content in a way that feels safe. It is often easier to write lyrics than to say something directly, and that small distance can help people explore difficult topics. In mental health settings, participants often enjoy songwriting activities more than verbal instruction and attend sessions more consistently because the process is engaging and personal (Backus, 2018).

Songwriting also supports people with dementia. It can help them reconnect with parts of themselves they may have forgotten and help caregivers see abilities they might have overlooked. Studies describe group songwriting as motivating, uplifting, and rewarding. It gives people opportunities to feel successful, participate more fully, and engage in creative and cognitive tasks (Backus, 2018).

The process of songwriting can be adjusted for anyone. A therapist might start with simple activities, such as replacing a few words in a familiar chorus or rewriting the lyrics to a well-known song. As clients grow more confident, they can move toward creating original music. Clients who do not play instruments can choose the feelings they want the music to convey while the therapist offers chord options, or they can use digital tools like GarageBand to design their own sound. Clients who play instruments can take the lead while the therapist provides support when it is needed.

Backus firmly believes that everyone is capable of writing a meaningful song. The act of creating music helps people feel heard, successful, and more connected to those around them. Songwriting offers a unique way for individuals to tell their stories and to see those stories turned into something lasting and powerful.

You meant to study, but instead, just one song can send your mind spiraling into memories, fantasies, or future plans. Sound familiar?

With a single melody, suddenly people can travel back in time, forward in dreams, away from reality. Cognitive neuroscientist Moshe Bar’s novel Mindwandering: How It Can Improve Your Mood and Boost Your Creativity discusses this phenomenon of our noisy, wandering minds. Mind wandering refers to letting one’s mind drift, and it is often the involuntary shifts in attention from a task at hand to internal thoughts. But is all mind wandering bad?

This seemingly idle mental activity is far from useless. Mind wandering is closely linked with the Default Mode Network, or DMN, which is a large-scale brain network of regions that are active when the brain is at “rest,” or when the brain is not focusing on a specific task at hand. Interestingly, the DMN occupies around 30–47% of people’s waking mental energy, and the brain is vigorously active in the DMN, often even more active than during experimental conditions. Often characterized by thinking about the self, others, the past, or future events, mind wandering is an intentional result of evolution that is pivotal for simulating future events, shaping well-being and identity, and more. Occurring in the DMN, which has a heavy focus on thinking of the past and future, mind wandering allows people to search their memories and create associations, helping people interpret life and acting as a form of predictive regulation.

Aside from functioning as a key proponent of human survival, mind wandering is often linked with boosting mood and creativity. Moshe Bar describes two states of mind: exploratory and exploitatory. The exploratory state of mind is more open-ended and imaginative. It relates to mind wandering, curiosity, novelty-seeking, and positive mood, and it is dominated by the DMN. On the other hand, a more task-focused and analytical form of thinking is associated with the exploitatory mode. Mindwandering helps shift out of the exploitatory mode and into more open-ended, mental exploration. 

Bar also notes that a positive mood leads to broader thinking, which in turn encourages more flexible and original ideas. Mood and mind wandering are, therefore, part of a loop that benefits each. While numerous prior studies have established the power of music in regulating mood and improving well-being, recent studies have been delving into the connection between mind wandering, mood, and music listening. In particular, a 2021 study conducted by Liila Taruffi utilizes an Experience Sampling Method (ESM) with a smartphone app, MuPsych, to capture mind wandering during everyday personal music listening. By tracking the participants’ moods, presence of mind wandering, and music-evoked emotions using the Geneva Emotional Music Scale (GEMS), the study finds that 57% of music episodes involved mind wandering, while mind wandering frequency was only at 36% for non-music episodes. In addition, the study finds that music significantly improved mood, and thoughts during music were often more positive than non-music, although not significantly so. The music-evoked emotions felt by the participant would therefore predict thought valence, meaning that positive emotions felt from listening to music would lead to positive thoughts, and negative emotions would lead to negative thoughts. Mood and thoughts influence each other, like a feedback loop. Since music can shift emotions, it thus impacts one’s thoughts, which then affects one’s mood again.

Music can help people shift into the exploratory mode, opening space for creativity and mood repair. In a world that often overvalues constant productivity, music invites us to wander and reconnect with ourselves.

Acapella singing, at first glance, might seem like a simple exercise in vocal harmony. There are no instruments, just voices interwoven to create melodies. But beneath this surface lies a deeply therapeutic practice. Much like how a concept album layers fictional characters and personal stories, an acapella group layers voices to express something greater than just the sum of its parts. When voices blend, individuals find not only music but also release, connection, and healing. In this way, acapella has carved a unique role in music therapy.

Unlike instruments that can be set down after use, the human voice is inseparable and always attached. To sing is to expose something raw, personal, and vulnerable. This is why therapists often turn to acapella as a tool in therapy: it strips away external distractions, leaving a pure human element. The act of singing with others and creating harmonies acts as a safe space for emotional release. For many, that act is as vulnerable as confession.

Much like narrative songwriting, acapella can tell stories of groups. Songs chosen in therapy often hold important symbolism or metaphors that participants can relate to and project onto. A song about resilience, for example, becomes more than melody. It becomes an anthem shared across voices, each singer contributing their story to its meaning.

Furthermore, science supports what singers feel intuitively. Singing in unison can regulate breathing, synchronize heartbeats, and trigger endorphin release. In a therapeutic context, this is extremely important. Controlled breathwork reduces anxiety, while synchronization fosters a sense of belonging. The art of acapella, with its focus on balance and blending, magnifies these effects.

Music therapists may incorporate acapella exercises in individual sessions, but its true strength often shows in group settings. Community choirs formed around mental health support provide spaces where participants are free from judgment, valued for their voice, regardless of training. For some, it becomes their first experience of being heard and accepted.

Acapella in music therapy is not about perfect pitch or polished performance. It is about finding voice, in every sense of the word. The therapeutic power lies in the act itself: the courage to sing, the willingness to listen, the trust to blend. Just as a layered album reveals itself only after multiple listens, the healing effects of an acapella emerge gradually. In the end, it is not just music; it is medicine.

If you play an instrument, you likely started playing it at a young age. In fact, most famous musicians we know of such as pianist Yuja Wang and composer Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart started their musical journeys as young children. So, why is it better to start learning an instrument as a child? What are the benefits? Not only is it easier for children to learn new skills, but studies have also established that there are cognitive benefits to learning music as a young child. 


Early childhood is a key time for brain development. Our young brains have many, many neurons that are ready for use. Each time we complete a new activity, a new connection in the brain is made, making that activity easier in the future. So, the repetitive practice involved in learning an instrument trains our brains to be faster and stronger. Specifically, learning an instrument can hone a child’s motor skills, coordination, and memory all at once. Do not underestimate the coordination needed to press and lift one’s fingers according to the music or the memory and attention needed to memorize a piece. Improvements in those aspects can be seen just after 14 months of musical training. A study observed that children ages 5-9 receiving weekly music lessons scored higher on tests corresponding to fine motor skills. In all, if you learned an instrument as a child, you had a head start to the cognitive game. 

Not only does learning an instrument give you a cognitive advantage in childhood, but it also keeps you ahead of the game throughout your life. When a group of study participants who played an instrument as a child took a cognitive test at ages 11 and 70, they scored higher than participants in the same experiment who didn’t have any musical experience. These participants had an advantage in spatial awareness, verbal skills, and numerical analysis. All the skills involved in playing an instrument keep the brain active and healthy, which can reduce the risk of brain-related illnesses later in life. Interestingly enough, some patients diagnosed with Alzheimer’s Disease or Dementia can remember how to play pieces on the instrument they learned many years ago, showing that the cognitive gain from learning an instrument sticks for life. 

Learning about an instrument’s cognitive benefits adds a whole new dimension of appreciation for it. Practicing an instrument can be tiring and tough, and it is easy to overlook the many benefits of being a musician; now you can also say you’re cognitively in good health!

Music comes in a multitude of different forms, whether that be through a live concert by your favorite artist who’s on their world tour right now, or going to see a live orchestra performance. Oftentimes, people tend to enjoy music on car rides, while reading, or when needing a distraction from an overwhelming amount of thoughts. But did you know that listening to music at night is most effective?

Think about the times when you were younger. Maybe you recall how your parents constantly read you books until you fell asleep or suggested that you count one hundred sheep in your head. But one of the most successful and scientifically proven methods to alleviate insomnia is through music. Listening to music can give the benefit of decreasing the amount of time it takes for someone to fall asleep. In 2006, the National Library of Medicine conducted a research study using three groups of students between the ages of 19 and 28 years with sleep complaints. Each group was provided with a different genre of music to listen to and the amount of time they should dedicate to listening to some sort of form of music before they slept; excluding the control group, who did not have any interruption or sounds, the two other groups were given classical music or an audiobook. 

Researchers were able to conclude that although the sleep quality of students did not improve significantly when comparing the audiobook with the control group, symptoms of depression remarkably decreased in the music group. Listening to calming classical music can help improve sleep quality, which makes it especially easier for school nurses because they can utilize this low-cost, safe, and simple approach in managing insomnia seen in students. 

As a result, music can mitigate tiredness and reduce stress, anxiety, and respiratory rate problems while also relieving muscle tension throughout the body. Devoting even just fifteen minutes to listening to soothing music before sleeping can help individuals shift into a relaxed state of mind. It is also important to keep in mind that audio devices worn over the ears while sleeping, such as headphones or earbuds, can ultimately result in ear canal damage and a higher risk of ear infections.  

Whilst there isn’t a specific genre of music an individual should listen to at night, it is highly recommended to stick with classical, ambient, folk, or jazz. This is because songs with a faster rhythm or pace can initiate strong emotional responses, which can interfere with a good night's sleep.

Dance therapy, a form of psychotherapy that involves using dance and movements to improve emotional and physical well-being, has been proven to help improve balance and coordination in those with Parkinson’s disease. This progressive neurological disorder affects body movement when certain nerve cells in the brain that produce dopamine gradually start degenerating.

Sherry Brown, a patient diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease, walked into her Dance for Parkinson’s Disease class at the Stanford Neuroscience Health Center. This was created for individuals struggling with body movements and speech, such as Sherry, to provide them with enjoyable dance sessions. After attending weeks of these sessions, she states that, “you get a sense of your body and are pushing your body to do things you don’t think you can accomplish.” Despite her condition, she still lives her life to the fullest, as she is a family therapist. When Sherry first found out that she was diagnosed with Parkinson’s, she felt devastated, almost as if “her life was over,” and it took a lot of time for her to completely process what was going on before she could accept this fact. Over time, her world slowly started to expand again as she began accepting her disease, through the support of physical therapy, medication, fitness training, and most importantly, dance. She began to regain her strength and move forward with healing. According to studies, participants in dance classes with Parkinson’s often show smoother walking, sharper senses of movement, and a noticeable boost in mood and confidence with knowing that they are able to feel more control over their bodies.  

The National Library of Medicine conducted a research study among individuals with and without Parkinson’s disease enrolled in dance classes to show a distinct comparison. In healthy older adults, it was found that walking speed increased by 0.05 m/s after dance classes. For people with Parkinson’s, dance interventions led to improvements in the 6-minute walk of 40-60 meters. To put that in perspective, a 20-meter improvement is already considered noticeable, but a 50-meter gain is seen as clinically meaningful.

Dance seems to have it all when it comes to exercise for people with Parkinson’s. It helps with flexibility, strength, and a cognitive boost for the brain as well. Most of the research has focused on those in the mild to moderate stages of Parkinson’s, but even spending some time dancing has shown many benefits. It remains unclear why exactly dance can work so well with individuals with Parkinson’s and how lasting those effects really are, but one thing’s clear: dance moves more than just the body, it elevates the mind and spirit as well!

Art therapy is an all-encompassing term used to describe the close connection between healing, creativity, sound, and movement. In many places around the world, a combination of these techniques is used to address pain management, cognitive behavioral problems, psychotherapy, and physical therapy, and it shows great results with people of all ages and backgrounds. But how can different types of art therapy be combined to form a more personal approach to recovery, happiness, and comfort in one’s own body?

Of all the forms of art therapy, dance and music seem to have the most in common. They both involve rhythm, emotional output, intricate movement, and are known to decrease anxiety and improve mood. Dance requires music, and music naturally leads to dance, creating the perfect opportunity for a versatile and customizable form of therapy.

The benefits of dance extend far beyond enjoyment, culture, and community. No matter your skill level, it can help boost physical and psychological well-being by building a positive body image and improving self-esteem, helping patients understand the extent of their capabilities and gain confidence. Dance can reduce anxiety, stress, and depression, alleviate isolation through collaboration, reduce chronic pain, and help release mental and physical tension. It is an exercise that demands effort from the entire body, requiring and producing strength, flexibility, and endurance, while increasing endorphins (pain relievers and mood boosters), strengthening circulatory and respiratory systems, and combining movement with joy and rhythm.

Music therapy, unsurprisingly, has many similar effects. The process of listening to music, making music (instrumental or vocal), or simply discussing it can have a remarkable impact on all aspects of one’s health. For seniors and hospitalized patients, it can help ease fear and stress, lower heart rate, blood pressure, and breathing rate, and promote relaxation and muscle tension relief. For people with mental health conditions, music can help with depression, sleeplessness, and emotional distress. But, in the end, it isn’t individual notes or dance moves that make these therapies so effective. It’s harmony, rhythm, feeling the beat, and experiencing a shared overflow of sensations that all lead back to healing.

Movement, just like music, is a universal language that connects people without words. It is our first language, one that aids in communication despite physical and emotional challenges, and fosters mutual understanding. So when every single person in the room listens to the same music and can feel and react to the rhythm, each person’s body (including their heart, along with other muscles) begins to synchronize to the beat. Whether it's a fast-paced pop song that creates an exciting energy and causes everyone to jump and twirl to the rhythm, or a leisurely classical piece with a beat similar to that of a resting human heart, endorphins are released and a balance is established throughout the entire body. Harmony, on the other hand, has an emotionally-centered impact. It emphasizes feelings, which can then be released through dance or processed separately. Music unveils the subconscious, and dance facilitates the comprehension of these emotions.

Music and dance therapy are separate yet entirely codependent processes. While each has its own benefits, purpose, and eventual outcome, they need one another to thrive. The goal of all art therapy is to make physical and psychological recovery more straightforward and accessible, and, consequently, any combination of approaches and techniques is progress toward more effective, enjoyable, and personalized healing. So if music is already a part of your journey, you might as well dance to it.

If you were to ask a child what they want to be when they grow up, chances are that a large percentage of them would respond with a “musician.” Now, more than ever, music has made its mark on pop culture and cemented itself as one of the most important aspects of day-to-day life, no matter what part of the world an individual is from. However, there is a grim reality beneath this idealized vision that many aspiring young musicians have. Problems such as meager payouts, lack of exposure, and unsustainability, have seeped their way into the music-sharing process. For this reason, we need to ask ourselves: how did we get to this position?

Think about today’s trending artists. Drake, the most listened-to artist of the 2010s has made over 52.5 million dollars from his Spotify earnings. That is impressive in and of itself, but try to guess the number of streams for his entire library of songs. It is estimated that over his entire 17-year career, he has accumulated about 28 billion streams. Doing the math, that’s about 0.002 dollars a stream. This means that every view that an artist receives, no matter their popularity, will amount to less than a cent. Even Drake is not safe from this sad reality; for reference, he earns 162 thousand dollars a month from Spotify. Now, most musicians will never reach the peaks that Drake has, which is exactly the problem. If an individual gathered, for instance, an average of 500 thousand listeners, using the conversion rate, that individual would earn a total of one thousand dollars per month. The data speak for themselves: the effort-to-reward ratio is astoundingly lower than it should be.

So, how do people circumvent this problem of not having a large enough following? There are many ways to do so, but the most common is to join an underground community to make connections. The first platforms that people think of that host these communities include SoundCloud, Bandcamp, and even YouTube. This may seem like a great way to slowly rise in the musical hierarchy and make a name for oneself–and oftentimes, it is. However, for the majority of people, this is the part of the journey when most musicians quit. This is because it is when they truly experience the fierce and ruthless environment of the music industry, which considers the smallest of skill gaps to be the determining factor to an artist’s success. Frequently, these up-and-coming musicians will have their music skyrocket to the top of the charts, leaving their roots as former creators of the alternative scenes. This can sometimes discourage those left behind who have been working for a long time and lead them to have artists’ blocks and question their own material. It is at this point when people begin to feel burnt out or hopeless about their abilities as artists end up entirely abandoning their careers: an option that crumbles any chance of success in the distant future.

Once these musicians reach the top, a whole new set of issues arises. Firstly, the artist can encounter a whole new set of expectations to consistently produce music at all times. These demands come from the newfound audience that they collect as a result of their recent popularity, and can often burn the artists out. In this scenario, the produced music starts to lack authenticity and quality. Additionally, the music industry’s mass appeal often prioritizes marketability over individuality, resulting in factory-produced and formulaic content that detracts from the humanity of the work. This affects the artist extremely negatively. Although the financial interest of the artist is met, their passion begins to dwindle. As these artists break their connections to the material, they often become detached from their own creations and lose interest in the medium overall.

Amidst these challenges, however, there is an opportunity for musicians to resist the societal temptations of manufactured and soulless music creation. By prioritizing creativity, authenticity, and connection to themselves, musicians can create their own unique paths in the industry, ignoring the typical roads to success. They can embrace alternate distribution channels, create genuine connections with the underground communities, and seek out audiences who value artistic integrity over commercial trends. 

It is essential for artists to realize that advancements in their status are not going to happen instantaneously. Developing perseverance and resilience will not only hone their craft, but also assist in reaching their goals of success in the future. After all, strong dedication to one’s craft can lead to long-term results. Normalizing a culture of originality will undoubtedly be a net positive for the music community, as everyone will be able to branch out and express themselves in the way they want.

Taylor Swift’s “Sweet Nothing” unfolds as a delicate reflection on the small, intimate moments that often go unnoticed in a chaotic world. Through her layered wordplay, Swift explores how the kind of love that asks for nothing can, in turn, mean everything.

Swift begins with the lines, “I spy with my little tired eye / Tiny as a firefly / A pebble that we picked up last July.” By referencing the iconic childhood game “I Spy,” she immediately evokes innocence and youth. Fireflies often symbolize fleeting, mirroring the brief and passing nature of sweet nothings, loving words quickly exchanged in whispers. At the same time, a firefly’s glow is a small light in darkness, which alludes to later themes of comfort amid turmoil: Swift, shrouded in difficulties, manages to find brightness in her lover.

Sweet nothings traditionally refer to the quiet, affectionate words exchanged between lovers that can sometimes be simple and sweet without carrying much profound meaning. When Swift references “the pebble [they] picked up,” which they “almost forgot,” she draws a parallel between the pebble’s insignificance and the simplicity of those whispers. Yet, despite the pebble’s trivial nature, she still remembers it, suggesting that even small moments or sweet nothings can leave lasting imprints.

The first meaning of “sweet nothing” becomes explicit in the chorus: “They said the end is comin' / Everyone’s up to somethin' / I find myself runnin' home to your sweet nothings.” Here, “the end” likely alludes to external predictions about her career, happiness, or personal life. In “Mirrorball,” Swift similarly references “the end” with “Hush, I know they said the end is near.” Amongst this external noise and anxiety, the detail of “runnin' home” conveys how her lover has become a safe space for her. In this moment, “sweet nothings” refers back to the traditional meaning: the comforting assurances and compliments from her partner.

Later in the chorus, Swift shifts into the second meaning, the crux of the song’s message: “Outside, they’re push and shovin' / You're in the kitchen hummin' / All that you ever wanted from me was sweet nothin'.” In these lines, Swift likely refers to the “outside” as an amalgamation of the loud, demanding world and the constant scrutiny and judgment she faces. The phrase “push and shovin'” echoes another common phrase, “when push comes to shove,” reinforcing the idea of how she feels pressured to act and follow the expectations of others. In contrast, her lover quietly hums, which is a carefree activity that embodies her lover’s tranquility and relieving simplicity. While the world wants more and more from Swift, her lover only wants “sweet nothing.” This comforting lack of expectation from her lover allows her to feel free to be herself and simply exist.

In the verse, Swift describes being surrounded by “Industry disruptors and soul deconstructors / And smooth-talking hucksters out glad-handing each other.” These figures represent people who demand more from her. More success, more output. She concludes by stating that with her partner, her “home,” she can admit she is “too soft for all of it,” revealing the vulnerability that she cannot show elsewhere. 

Although many speculate about the song’s subject, this interpretation centers on the song as a love letter at its core. The second verse reinforces this idea, referencing Paul McCartney’s tweet about his relationship with his wife, Linda. Swift writes, “On the way home / I wrote a poem / You say, 'What a mind’ / This happens all the time.” McCartney’s tweet mentions that when he shared his poems with Linda, she would respond with the phrase “What a mind”—the same expression Swift quotes in her lyrics. McCartney further explains in his tweet that Linda genuinely meant her praise; it was not just empty flattery but genuine and heartfelt admiration. Similarly, Swift uses this example to highlight how she regards her lover’s “sweet nothings” as sincere and affirming rather than meaningless.

While sweet nothings are often fleeting or forgettable, both McCartney’s anecdote and Swift’s lyrics defy the conventions of the phrase “sweet nothings,” emphasizing how these truly heartfelt small words linger. Even things meant to be “nothing” can become meaningful.

Other interpretations propose that the song is dedicated to her mother or that it carries a sadder undertone. Some analyses highlight the lyrical shift from “sweet nothings” to “nothin’” in the second chorus, suggesting a commentary on the emptiness or limitations of wanting nothing. Ultimately, the beauty of songs and their lyrics lies in their ability to resonate differently with each listener, as each person can find their own meaning within Swift’s words.

“Who Knows” by Daniel Caesar is an intimate admittance of insecurity, so heartfelt that it feels like listening to a private conversation. Its serene vocals and light guitar strums highlight the raw, powerful lyrics, in which Caesar grapples with the inevitable feeling of being unable to get into his lover’s head and understand her thoughts. 

"I'll probably be a waste of your time, but who knows? / Chances are I'll step out of line, but who knows? / Lately, you've set up in my mind / Yeah, girl, you, and I like that"

Caesar is beginning to fall in love. However, he immediately starts the song with a ponderous question. It is a game of possibility: he preemptively deems himself a disappointment in preparation for facing the possibility of failure; yet, there is also the possibility that he could be the right one. There is an undertone of inevitable disappointment, as Caesar believes he is the kind of person who will eventually fail his lover. The girl setting up in his mind is a gentle take on the power love has to consume one’s mind. By saying he likes it, Caesar is attempting to come to terms with the fact that he is losing control.

"Lately, I've been thinking that perhaps I am a coward / Hiding in a disguise of an ever-giving flower / Incompetent steward of all of that sweet, sweet power"

Caesar calls himself a coward for hiding behind the image of being an “ever-giving flower” who can readily radiate love and is selfless. In reality, he is afraid to be emotionally vulnerable and express his insecurities to his lover. He is scared to ruin the relationship by being himself, hence the facade.

"Yesterday was feeling so good, now it's gone / I'd feel like that always if I could, is that wrong? / Tell me 'bout the city you're from / Is it hot? Does it snow there?"

Caesar is holding onto the feeling of yesterday, a fleeting moment of the past. He asks if it’s wrong to want to experience that happiness again because he yearns for a feeling that’s slipping away, and it would be selfish to hold onto it. He tries to stall the moment by asking empty questions.

"Lately, I've been thinking 'bout my precarious future / Will you be there with me by my side, my girl, my shooter? / Who's to say who calculates? Not me, I'm no computer"

Caesar again references an uncertain future, thus questioning if his girl will be by his side. He calls his girl his “shooter” because she can protect him when he can’t protect himself. However, he immediately second-guesses himself by saying he doesn’t have the logic or formulas to “calculate” the outcome of his relationship. The theme of losing control continues: Caesar has lost a logical foothold on himself and the relationship. He now relies on instinct and emotion to navigate this love.

"Is it a crime to be unsure? (Let me know, let me know, let me know, let me) / In time we'll find (Let me know, let me know, let me know, let me) / If it's sustainable (Let me know, let me know, let me know, let me) / You're pure, you're kind (Let me know, let me know, let me know, let me) / Mature, divine (Let me know, let me know, let me know, let me) / You might be too good for me, unattainable (Let me know, let me know, let me know, let me)"

By calling uncertainty a crime, Caesar not only doubts the future of his relationship but also his humanity. The repetition of “let me know” is a gentle plea for his lover to give him closure to his uncertainty. He wants her to be upfront with her perspective on him and their relationship. He puts his lover on a pedestal, describing her as someone so “divine” he can barely reach her. Even if his lover is unattainable, he still wants to stay and wait out the possibilities. 

"Maybe we get married one day, but who knows? / Think I'll take that thought to the grave, but who knows? / I know that I'll love you always / Yeah, girl you, and I'd like that"

Caesar would rather die believing in the possibility of what his relationship could be than live knowing a shattering truth. He is not calling himself cowardly for not wanting to face the truth; rather, he accepts that he must cohabitate with uncertainty and vulnerability. 

Throughout the song, Caesar turns a “who knows” of agonizing uncertainty into a “who knows” of acceptance. He is willing to wholly devote himself to his lover when he is insecure in their relationship and in himself. Despite his passionate yearning for love, Caesar chose to produce “Who Knows” as a quiet self-reflection, highlighting the intricate contrasts of navigating uncertainty in a relationship: self-deprecating yet losing self-control, wanting closure yet possibility, and staying out of love despite it all.

In the summer of 1975, audiences lined up to see the movie Jaws, and many left the theater afraid to go back in the water. While the mechanical shark terrified viewers, it was John Williams’ unforgettable score “bah-dump…bah-dump…BAH-DUMP” that heightened the dread. This theme is a classic example of how music in horror films intensifies suspense, primes emotions, and heightens fear (Williams, 1975).

Music has long been a tool for building tension in drama, from operas to ballets to cinema. As music scholar Neil Lerner explains, “Music contributes a lot to the overall emotional experience of an audience” (Lerner in Chills & Thrills). Composers employ rhythm, dynamics, pitch, and instrumentation to manipulate how viewers feel.

One of the most common devices is rhythm. A quickening beat, resembling a racing heartbeat, can signal pursuit, while an irregular pulse suggests that something is dangerously “off” (Grieg, 1875). Similarly, dynamics play a major role: soft, eerie passages build suspense, and sudden loud bursts, known as “stingers,” deliver shock.

Pitch also heightens anxiety. Just as voices rise when people are frightened, composers use ascending notes to convey panic. Schubert’s “Der Erlkönig” (1821) exemplifies this technique. Dissonance, especially the tritone or “Devil’s Interval,” creates sonic discomfort by clashing sound waves. Historically dubbed “Diabolus in Musica,” the tritone appears in Camille Saint-Saëns’ Danse Macabre (1874).

Instrumentation adds another eerie layer. The waterphone, theremin, and pipe organ produce sounds so uncanny that they have become staples of horror scores (Law, 2023). Even prepared pianos generate alien tones, as explored by John Cage and George Crumb.

Why does scary music affect us so strongly? The answer lies in the brain. The amygdala, a structure responsible for processing fear, is highly responsive to unsettling sounds. A 2005 Oxford study revealed that people missing this region struggled to recognize scary music, while those with intact amygdalas reacted instinctively (Chills & Thrills). Moreover, evolutionary biology plays a role: nonlinear sounds, like human screams or distorted effects, mimic animal distress calls, triggering a primal alarm (Law, 2023).

Whether through the ominous Jaws theme or a sinister violin trill, horror music manipulates both body and brain. As Lerner suggests, our instincts hear the score as a predator closing in, and we shiver and brace ourselves for what’s to come.

Frank Ocean’s channel ORANGE is a metaphorical masterpiece, weaving together fictional elements to tell the story of the summer he first fell in love with a man at the age of 19. Each song should be listened to multiple times to appreciate its depth, and a single surface-level listen just isn’t enough. Through the seemingly disconnected lenses of a rich but isolated teenager in “Super Rich Kids,” a man losing his “queen” (girlfriend) to prostitution using Cleopatra as a metaphor in “Pyramids,” a man using his girlfriend as a drug mule in “Lost,” and Jenny in “Forrest Gump,” Frank weaves a beautiful narrative of his overwhelming emotional state, with these narratives flipping like TV “channels.” Frank associates these emotions with the color orange through synesthesia, a condition where feelings and senses are intertwined. The beauty of this album lies in its imaginative freedom of interpretation, but delving into specific songs gives the listener a window into Frank’s mind. 

While many songs of channel ORANGE contain fictional elements, “Bad Religion” is strikingly personal. This poignant ballad to a taxi driver about Frank’s struggle with his sexuality is vulnerable and raw, with “Bad Religion” as a metaphor for unrequited love. Frank uses sharp comparisons of a “one-man cult” and “cyanide in [his] styrofoam cup” (a reference to the Jonestown Massacre, where Reverend Jim Jones tricked his followers into drinking poisoned Kool-Aid from styrofoam cups) to show the depth and despair of an unrequited love. However, the song can also be seen as an unrequited love for a God who won’t accept him for his sexuality. In fact, a declaration of homosexuality can be a huge career hit for a top R&B artist like Frank. More broadly, many listeners who have had similar experiences of persecution due to sexuality, religion, or race can identify with Frank’s authenticity in “Bad Religion.”

In contrast, “Lost,” a hit song on the album, is more upbeat and tells the story of using a lover as a drug mule. The lover becomes “lost in the heat of it all,” unable to pry themselves from this lifestyle, being able to travel anywhere: “Miami, Amsterdam, Tokyo, Spain, lost…” The song could be about being lost in what one loves in general, suggested by the ending, where Frank blends the words “love” and “lost.” However, is it really love one is lost in, or the allure? For the lover in Frank’s song, it’s the lifestyle. But that allure could be something different to each one of Frank’s millions of listeners. 

With 17 songs and 55 minutes, channel ORANGE is multidimensional. While the listener is taken on a journey and transported from one scene to the next, Frank’s storytelling element and authenticity still shine through. It is a deep listen, beyond just enjoying the music, although his vocals and production warrant a listen in their own right. Frank’s story is both personal and interpretive, resonating with listeners in different ways and earning its popularity and title.

Global events shape music trends because artists respond to the world around them — not just creatively, but emotionally and politically. While Illustrate Magazine (September 5, 2025) highlights how major historical moments like wars and economic crises influence genres, the broader pattern shows that music evolves alongside shifts in identity, technology, and communication (Illustrate Magazine, 2025). 

For example, the rise of jazz in the 1920s was not only a reaction to post–World War I optimism, but was also part of the Harlem Renaissance. This larger cultural movement celebrated Black identity and artistic innovation. Similarly, the folk music of the Great Depression reflected economic struggle and also helped build a tradition of storytelling in American music that continues in modern genres like indie and country. These examples show that music does more than react to events. It preserves cultural identity and carries ideas forward across generations.

Global conflicts have repeatedly turned music into a tool for unity and resistance. During World War II, swing music boosted morale. However, music also became a form of propaganda and national identity. In later decades, protest music during the Vietnam War did not just reflect public opinion — it actively shaped it, influencing how younger generations engaged with politics and activism. This demonstrates that music can both respond to events and influence their outcomes.

Technological change is another key factor that extends beyond the article’s discussion. While the Cold War era introduced electronic music, the digital revolution of the 2000s fundamentally changed how music spreads. Streaming platforms and social media allow songs to go viral globally within hours, meaning modern music trends are shaped not only by events but by how quickly those events are shared and discussed online. For instance, political protests today often have soundtracks that gain traction on platforms like TikTok, blending activism with digital culture.

Globalization has also made music more interconnected than ever. The article notes the rise of world music, but today’s trends go even further. Genres like K-pop and Afrobeat dominate international charts, showing how global audiences now shape what becomes popular. This shift reflects a world where cultural exchange happens instantly, and music no longer belongs to a single region or audience.
