Music therapy is more than listening to your favorite songs; it’s a scientifically backed practice with some unexpected benefits and a long history. While many people know that music can improve your mood and reduce stress, many other facts about music therapy are less well-known. 
	
One of the most interesting aspects of music therapy is its connection to heart health. Studies have shown that listening to certain types of music can synchronize with heart rhythms, helping to regulate blood pressure and improve cardiovascular health. In some cases, music therapy has been used to maintain heart rates in patients recovering from heart surgery. The heart is not the only area that music affects. Another surprising fact is that music therapy can help people with Parkinson’s disease regain their mobility. Parkinson’s disease is a neurodegenerative disorder that affects a person’s movement, balance, and coordination. Since rhythm is processed in a different part of the brain than voluntary movement, patients who struggle with walking can often move better while listening to music with a steady beat. Known as rhythmic auditory stimulation, this technique helps people with movement disorders move more smoothly and maintain better balance. Alzheimer’s disease, another neurodegenerative disorder, affects memory and thinking. It has been shown that these patients may suddenly be able to remember lyrics, melodies, or even memories when listening to songs from their past.
	
Music therapy has also been used as a tool for pain management during childbirth. Some hospitals have introduced music therapy programs in maternity wards, allowing mothers to use their playlists to manage labor pain naturally. The rhythm and melody of their choice of songs can help distract from pain while also promoting relaxation, and therefore allowing the body to naturally deal with pain. 
	
Humans aren’t the only ones who benefit from music therapy. Some veterinarians and animal shelters use calming music to reduce anxiety in dogs, cats, and even horses. Specifically, classical music has been found to lower stress levels in animals, making them more comfortable in stressful environments.
	
One of the most unexpected uses of music therapy is in the surgical setting. Some hospitals have experimented with using music therapy instead of general anesthesia for minor procedures, allowing patients to stay awake, yet relaxed, during surgery. While this practice is still highly limited, early research shows that music can lower anxiety and pain perception, enough to reduce the need for heavy sedatives.
	
From improving mobility to easing pain and even benefiting animals, music therapy is a fascinating field with endless applications and potential. Its ability to heal and transform lives continues to be studied and applied in new creative ways, proving that music is an all-around way of healing.

Periods of change and uncertainty can make people feel overwhelmed, anxious, or unsure of how to interpret their experiences. Throughout history, people have turned to art during difficult or transitional moments, whether through painting, music, literature, or other forms of creative expression. Art offers a way to reflect, express emotions, and find meaning when words alone are not enough. Scientific research and psychological studies increasingly show that art is not only enjoyable but also plays a powerful role in helping individuals process complex emotions and navigate uncertain times.

One reason art helps people cope with change is the way it affects the brain. Research shows that viewing art can stimulate the release of dopamine, a neurotransmitter associated with pleasure and emotional well-being. This chemical response can produce feelings similar to those experienced when people fall in love, creating a sense of calm and satisfaction. Because of this effect, simply looking at artwork that resonates with a person can reduce stress and improve mood (“Why Do People Enjoy Art?”). In uncertain times, when anxiety and stress often increase, this neurological response can help stabilize emotions and provide a moment of mental relief.
Creating art can have an even deeper impact on the brain. Activities such as drawing, painting, or sculpting strengthen neural connections across both hemispheres of the brain. These processes enhance observation, memory, and problem-solving while also encouraging creativity and imagination (“Why Do People Enjoy Art?”). Art making also provides a nonverbal outlet for complex feelings. When people struggle to articulate emotions such as fear, confusion, or grief, creative expression can communicate those feelings in ways that language cannot. This expressive freedom can help individuals better understand their experiences and gradually make sense of uncertain situations.

Psychological research further suggests that art encourages introspection, which is especially important during periods of change. When individuals engage deeply with meaningful art, a region of the brain known as the default mode network becomes active. This system is associated with reflection, daydreaming, and thinking about oneself and the future. Because of this connection, interacting with art can prompt people to examine their thoughts, memories, and emotions more closely. In times of uncertainty, this inward reflection allows individuals to interpret events, reconsider their perspectives, and gradually develop a clearer understanding of their place in the world.

Art can also lead to transformative emotional experiences. Researchers studying aesthetic experiences have found that art can evoke a wide range of reactions, from calmness and pleasure to discomfort and challenge. These responses sometimes lead to what researchers call “small transformations,” in which viewers gain insight or learn something new about themselves. In other cases, art can produce deeper shifts that challenge a person’s worldview and encourage personal growth. While these experiences may initially feel uncomfortable, they can ultimately help individuals adapt to change by expanding their understanding of complex issues and emotions.

Another reason art helps people process uncertainty is its ability to foster empathy and connection. Artistic works often communicate personal emotions and experiences that others can relate to. When viewers recognize those emotions, they may feel less isolated in their own struggles. Studies show that meaningful engagement with art can increase empathy, strengthen social bonds, and promote cross-cultural understanding. In uncertain times, this shared emotional experience can remind people that their feelings are part of a broader human experience.

Art also slows people down and encourages mindfulness. In a fast-paced world filled with constant information and change, people often move quickly from one task to another without reflecting on their emotional state. Engaging with art invites individuals to pause, observe details, and consider how a work makes them feel. This process of careful attention can create a moment of presence and self-awareness. By slowing down and focusing on the experience, people can become more aware of their own emotions and better able to process them.

Ultimately, art provides both emotional relief and intellectual insight during uncertain times. It allows individuals to express difficult feelings, reflect on their experiences, and connect with others through shared emotions. Scientific research shows that art can stimulate positive neurological responses, strengthen cognitive abilities, and encourage introspection and empathy. Together, these effects make art a powerful tool for navigating the challenges of change.

While uncertainty is an inevitable part of life, art offers a meaningful way to face it. Through both creation and observation, art allows people to explore their inner worlds, understand their emotions, and discover new perspectives. In doing so, it transforms confusion and uncertainty into opportunities for reflection, growth, and connection.

If you walk through a gym, you may notice a large majority of exercisers wearing headphones of some sort. Why is it that most people prefer to listen to music while exercising? Christopher Ballmann’s review, “The Influence of Music Preference on Exercise Responses and Performance: A Review,” shows that people of all fitness levels perform better, both physically and mentally, when listening to music they enjoy. Take Tara, a fellow high school student who frequents the gym. She says that listening to hype beats while working out motivates her and gives her more energy. 

Tara notes that she physically feels more energized when listening to music. Studies have found changes in neuronal activity in the brain associated with increased coordination and movements. In addition, studies have shown that listening to fast-paced music may increase blood flow to the muscles, which increases performance during exercise. Psychologically, individuals who listen to music while exercising feel more motivated. Ballmann’s review notes that having “positive” feelings during exercise is linked to increased endurance and higher exercise intensity. Music enhances positive emotions, energy, and alertness—factors that contribute to greater endurance, workout intensity, and motivation. He notes that these findings apply to just about anyone, whether you're a professional athlete or someone looking to get fit. Therefore, listening to music combats the fatigue and negative feelings that result from strenuous exercise and keeps the exerciser motivated and invigorated.

Another classmate once noted that she listens to more mellow songs when working out, which was surprising since songs with faster tempos are generally considered more stimulating for exercise. So, is the formula for the genre of music and increased physical activity the same for everyone? Scientific American affirms the negative. What makes music motivating depends on whether it evokes a rhythm response, or how much the music makes people want to move. Cultural diversity profoundly influences the field of music therapy, shaping its practices and enhancing therapeutic outcomes. In today’s increasingly multicultural societies, music therapists are called upon to integrate diverse cultural perspectives into their interventions to promote healing and inclusivity.

 Defining Cultural Diversity in Music Therapy

Culture encompasses the collective beliefs, customs, arts, and social institutions of a group of people. In music therapy, cultural diversity refers to the array of cultural backgrounds that therapists and clients bring to the therapeutic setting. Recognizing and valuing these differences is essential for building rapport and delivering effective treatment. As noted in Music Therapy in a Multicultural Context, understanding and integrating various cultural and social identities into practice enables therapists to effectively meet the needs of diverse clients (Belgrave and Kim 15).

 Historical Context

Music has served as a healing tool across various cultures for millennia. In ancient Greece, music was integral to healing rituals; similarly, African traditions have long utilized music and dance to promote spiritual and physical well-being. These practices underscore the universal significance of music in healing and have laid the groundwork for contemporary music therapy.

 Cultural Considerations in Music Therapy Practice

Incorporating cultural considerations into music therapy involves understanding clients’ cultural contexts, including their musical preferences, identities, and health beliefs. This approach ensures that therapy is relevant and respectful. For example, integrating traditional songs from a client’s culture can enhance engagement and provide comfort. As highlighted in Music Therapy in a Multicultural Context, therapists are encouraged to integrate understanding of different cultural and social identities into their practice to effectively meet the needs of diverse clients (Belgrave and Kim 15).

 Developing Multicultural Competence

Developing multicultural competence is a lifelong journey involving education, self-reflection, and practical experience. Therapists must be aware of their own cultural biases and strive to understand the cultural contexts of their clients. The American Music Therapy Association emphasizes the importance of cultural competence, stating that therapists should “strive to achieve multicultural competence through a lifelong journey of formal and informal education and self-reflection.” This journey towards cultural competence is essential in addressing the diverse needs of clients and in providing effective music therapy interventions.

 Applications of Culturally Responsive Music Therapy

Culturally responsive music therapy has been applied in various settings. For instance, hip-hop therapy has been used as a culturally relevant approach to engage African American adolescents in mental health treatment. This approach utilizes elements of hip-hop culture, such as rap and spoken word, to facilitate expression and address psychological issues (Tyson 131). Additionally, music therapy has been effectively employed in palliative care settings, incorporating cultural music preferences to enhance the quality of life for terminally ill patients (O’Brien 9). In community settings, culturally tailored music therapy programs have been developed to engage diverse populations, demonstrating the versatility and effectiveness of these approaches.

 Challenges and Opportunities

Integrating cultural diversity into music therapy presents challenges, such as the need for ongoing education and potential language barriers. Therapists may encounter difficulties in understanding the cultural contexts of their clients, which can impede the therapeutic process. However, embracing cultural diversity offers opportunities to enrich therapeutic practices. By incorporating a variety of cultural perspectives, music therapists can enhance client engagement, promote inclusivity, and improve therapeutic outcomes. As the population becomes increasingly diverse, the demand for culturally responsive music therapy practices will continue to grow, highlighting the importance of ongoing education and adaptation in the field.

 Conclusion

Cultural diversity is integral to the practice of music therapy. By acknowledging and incorporating the rich tapestry of cultural backgrounds, music therapists can provide more effective, empathetic, and inclusive care. This approach not only enhances the healing experience for clients from all walks of life but also enriches the therapists’ understanding and appreciation of the diverse cultural landscapes they navigate.

The compact disc (CD) is a physical plastic disc that typically contains some form of digital media. The way that it is created is through a laser beam, which scans the top for the reproduction of sounds or anything else. Although at one point in time the CD was considered practical and a new convenient invention, today it is considered lost. At one point, however, the compact disc was considered for beyond audio recordings and other storage–distribution usages. With its municipal purposes, along with its new storage, the CD was considered a trailblazer during its time. 

History & Rise of the CD

The CD was first developed by Sony and Philips on August 31st, 1982, in Tokyo. The invention of the CD–12 cm compact audio disc and a CD player quickly rose to fame due to its convenience and partnerships with record labels and CD manufacturers that enticed them to push its promotion further, as CDs were the successors of other older forms of physical media of music, such as vinyl. By the year 1985, roughly 25 million CDs and 5 million CD players had been sold. The CD, after gaining so much traction and popularity, moved onto other platforms of applications, which served as the standard for multiple innovations. From this point on, the CD was considered a household staple that many used. Artists and record labels pushed out personal CDs carrying music on this new audio format – it was the hot new thing of the time. 

Fall of the CD

However, in the early 2000s, the fall of physical media started after other inventions of convenience were created. In particular, CDs were being replaced by other forms of digital storage. This resulted in CDs being dropped by around 50% of their peak. Specifically in the United States, it was found by the High Resolution & Digital Audio that the sales of physical media in the year 2023 dropped by 10.5%. Streaming services became more and more popular as the years went on, such as Spotify and Apple Music. Today, the global market of music is growing with digital downloads increasing further, and the use of physical media such as CDs decreasing. With this, CDs are slowly becoming forgotten by the new generation. Yet, internationally, CDs are still holding on, such as in Germany, where they are still considered the strongest format with 12.9% in revenue. In such international countries, the CD has the chance to still live on for others to use.

During this time, K-pop began to heavily incorporate R&B, electronic sounds, and Western hip-hop influences. Technological advancements have also played a significant role in shaping K-pop’s trajectory. The rise of social media, YouTube, and various streaming platforms made it easier for K-pop groups to build and engage with international fanbases. High-concept music videos, intricate choreography, and bite-sized promotional content have become essential elements of a group’s brand.

The narrative of K-pop is one of creative evolution and adaptation. By merging global influences with distinct Korean cultural elements, the industry has crafted a unique and innovative musical landscape. Each generation has built upon the last, transforming K-pop from a domestic trend into a global powerhouse. Today, K-pop isn't merely a reflection of Korean pop music; it embodies a new model of worldwide pop culture, defined by fusion, performance, and an unyielding drive for reinvention.

When considering the peaks of the classical music era and what works came out of it, composers such as Mozart and Beethoven might pop up in one’s mind. While those composers are considered significant landmarks in the timeline of classical music, a criminally underrated one is Franz Joseph Haydn, nicknamed the father of the symphony. Haydn shaped the musical landscape that later composers would build upon. 

Childhood and Adolescence 

Missa brevis in F major 

In the early 1730s, like many composers, Haydn was born into a musical family in Rohrau, Austria. However, Haydn hadn’t been born into a life of extravagance. Haydn’s father and mother were commoners and worked as wheelwrights and cooks, respectively. Despite their modest backgrounds, both demonstrated an interest in music, which encouraged Haydn’s own passion. Even as a child, Haydn’s potential and talent were recognized. 

In the present day, Haydn is more widely known for his symphonies and other compositions. While Haydn was talented in playing the violin and the harpsichord, he was praised for his wondrously beautiful soprano voice. At the age of six, Haydn was sent to live with a family member in Hainburg. It was there that he trained in music theory. However, the conditions he lived in were far from glamorous. It is said that Haydn’s physical needs were frequently left unmet, being frequently beaten and starved during his stay in Hainburg with the Frankh family. 

Haydn remained in Hainburg for about two years until he was recognized by a musical director who was impressed enough to offer him a position in his choir. This prompted a move to Vienna, where he performed in the choir of St. Stephan’s Cathedral. However, at the age of seventeen, Haydn was expelled from the choir and the school he attended due to multiple reasons. One of the more prevalent reasons behind his dismissal was his vocal change. To preserve young males’ voices, during Haydn’s era, many pre-pubescent boys underwent castration. There are many contradicting accounts, some claiming that Haydn was about to undergo the procedure before being stopped by his father, who came to Vienna to intervene. Others near Haydn contest that claim and say that Haydn himself refused to be castrated. Regardless, Haydn’s inability to sing soprano, his poor grades, and an alleged misdemeanor with a classmate, Haydn was forced to leave. 

Missa brevis, translated to “short mass,” was one of the earliest authenticated pieces written by Haydn. It was said to have been written before or shortly after Haydn’s dismissal from the cathedral. While experts are almost certain that the Missa brevis is not Haydn’s absolute first work, it is the earliest that was discovered and officiated. Missa brevis in F major is a mass, featuring a choral and string part. While the mass is not considered the best or particularly masterful, it showcases Haydn’s emerging talent and potential in composing music despite his youth and inexperience. 

Young Adulthood

Der krumme Teufel 

After being sent out, Haydn began working multiple musical jobs in Vienna, which included being a street musician, an accompanist, and a teacher. Among many other professions, he worked as a composer. During the early 1750s, he wrote a comedic opera called “Der krumme Teufel”, translated to “The Limping Devil.” Although the original score of the music has been lost, its existence is known due to the script of the opera. Additionally, multiple revised editions of the opera have been found with varying names. The opera was written during the early 1750s and performed years later.

Despite the success of his first satirical opera, Haydn deeply struggled upon his dismissal from the cathedral. However, with the help of various mentors, a notable one being Nicola Porpora, an Italian composer and teacher. Although Haydn had learned music theory from the choir school he attended previously, in comparison, it was quite minimal. Later, Haydn praises Porpora for being the mentor he needed and teaching him proper technique in both composition and singing. 

With the assistance of Porpora and other mentors, Haydn improved greatly. Due to this, he connected with other well-known composers of the era, including J.S. Bach’s son, Carl Emanuel Bach, whom Haydn spoke highly of. It is because of these formative years that he was able to become a composer and create some of his greatest works later on. 

Middle Age 

Symphony No. 45 in F-sharp minor ("Farewell")

Haydn was famously named the “Father of the Symphony” due to the sheer amount he wrote during his lifetime. Due to the era in which Haydn was born, there are discrepancies when counting the symphonies completed by Haydn due to potential cataloging errors and lost repertoire. However, most historians agree that he wrote around one hundred and six symphonies. The first of which that was confirmed to have been written by him, was composed in the early 1760s or late 1750s when Haydn was just twenty-seven years old.

This was also around the time when he married Maria Anna Keller. Reportedly, their marriage was an unhappy one. Although it remains unconfirmed, the reason behind Haydn’s contempt for his wife, a reasonable assumption is that he did not want to marry her at all and deemed her incompatible, as he initially desired Maria’s younger sister, Therese, who opted to become a nun. Karl Geiringer, a historian known for his book Haydn: A Creative Life in Music, comments that Haydn’s musical artistry was seemingly affected by the lack of emotional stability and love from within his marriage. It is also reported that Maria was not interested in music and was indifferent to it. In Geiringer’s book, he says, “If anything in Haydn’s personal life were responsible for these unrestrained outbursts, it was not the excess, but rather the starvation of his emotional life.” Additionally, historians speculate that the bulk of Haydn’s consistent discontent was due to his wife’s infertility, coupled with their incompatibility.

Perhaps due to the emotional turmoil within his marriage and private life, Haydn’s work suffered a drastic change in terms of expression and technique. Haydn wrote his forty-fifth symphony, nicknamed Farewell. It was named as such due to the story of why the composer wrote the symphony. Haydn and the musicians who first performed the symphony had been staying at Prince Nikolaus Esterházy’s palace for an extended period of time, which caused many of the musicians to long for home. The hope of returning was quickly snuffed out, however, when the prince kept requesting them to extend their stay, which kept the musicians away from their families. To persuade the prince to do otherwise, Haydn wrote the symphony and arranged for the musicians to stop playing and leave one by one until only two musicians remained. The message was conveyed successfully, as the musicians and Haydn were permitted to leave and visit their families. 

The instance was just one example of how Haydn’s clever wit even managed to seep its way into his music, and was demonstrated in the forty-fifth symphony and his later works. Haydn had masterfully convinced his employer to release his musicians through wordless communication. 

Golden Age

Paris Symphonies (Symphonies 82~87)

The 1770s and 1780s marked a stylistic change where Haydn began branching out into different forms of music. Said shift heavily altered the classical music genre as a whole and redefined it. This part of his life produced more symphonies, string quartets, trios, and operas than ever before. This period was also significant in his personal life, as Haydn settled in his late forties.

Haydn was also famously known for being childless, attributed to the infertility of his wife. For numerous reasons, both Haydn and his wife took extramarital lovers, as divorce wasn’t legalized in this era. Because of this, it trapped the couple within the confines of their frigid and loveless marriage. Haydn’s eyes began to wander and landed on the beautiful and young mezzo-soprano, Luigia Polzelli. A thing to note is that Luigia, Haydn’s mistress, was married to a violinist named Antonio Polzelli, who had been prematurely dismissed from his job in 1779. According to Geiringer, Haydn felt sympathy for the young singer before it transformed into love. While practically nothing is known about Luigia, aside from her love affair with the famed composer, what is known is that she likely produced Haydn’s illegitimate child, Alois Anton Nikolaus Polzelli. Although Haydn never claimed either child as his own, he apparently loved both, taught them music, and supported them financially. 

Notably, around this time, Haydn met Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart in 1783. Both became fascinated with one another and became friends. While they had known of each other, they had never formally met prior to the 1780s. Despite Mozart’s overwhelming talent, Haydn was reportedly not jealous and respected him deeply. Mozart returned the same admiration, dedicating six of his string quartets to Haydn, and affectionately calling him a mentor. Their personalities differed greatly, Mozart being emotionally turbulent and passionate, while Haydn was famously calm and modest, in comparison to Mozart’s boastful nature. Both possessed witty and cheeky qualities that they likely bonded over. 

It is during this era of his life that he produced his best works, such as his Paris Symphonies, which were commissioned during the mid-1780s. The five secular symphonies were praised for being new, fresh, and dramatic. They represented Haydn’s vast musical range within the movements. Rightfully so, these symphonies were widely praised and were extremely popular for their genius. 

Golden Age

Symphony No.94 “Surprise”

During the 1790s, critics agree that this was his golden era of compositions, most of his greatest works being released during this time. After the death of his cherished patron, Prince Nikolaus, the majority of the musicians within the former prince’s court were dissolved and dismissed. As stated by Geiringer in his biography, Haydn had been eager to leave Eszterháza, and leaped at the opportunity to venture to London. 

On the way to London, he famously met Ludwig van Beethoven, who was in his mid-20s. Impressed by the young musician’s work, Haydn moved Beethoven to Vienna to study with him. Their personalities, however, clashed heavily because of Beethoven’s fiery temper. Beethoven was known to be very rebellious, combative, and irritable. These lessons took place during Haydn’s phase of traveling, forcing Beethoven to seek lessons elsewhere in Haydn’s absence. However, Beethoven famously sought out Haydn’s advice on his third trio, which Haydn criticized, leaving a lasting impact on Beethoven. Despite the friction caused by the criticism he received, the two remained cordial, and Beethoven later dedicated some work to his old teacher. One that perfectly displayed the composer’s humorous personality was his ninety-fourth symphony, nicknamed “The Surprise Symphony.” It was nicknamed so because of its large chord in the middle of a quiet movement, intended to startle his audience. 

After settling back down in Vienna, Haydn shifted away briefly from symphonies, refocusing on choral and nonsecular music, inspired by Handel’s work. 

Near the End

String Quartet Op.103 

Towards the end of the 18th century, Haydn’s health took a turn for the worse, but his music production had yet to cease. The composer managed to compose The Creation and The Seasons. It was during this decade that he drew closer and closer to his death. In 1808, a grand performance of his work, The Creation, was held for his birthday. The prolific was attended by members of the royal family and numerous musicians, including his old student, Beethoven. While this event was incredibly touching and was a grand gesture, it severely exhausted him. 

Haydn spent his final years in Vienna, slowly weakened by illness and left unable to compose. The composer became more heavily reliant on the assistance of servants and friends, and many of his works were left unfinished for that reason. Haydn was no longer the energetic creator he once was. He became confined to his home in Vienna, slowly becoming aware that his days of composing music were over. The slow progression to his death was most definitely gutting and profound, as he had been composing for his entire life. His final incomplete work was String Quartet Op.103, consisting of only two movements, before his health rendered him unable to compose. Although his physical state was deteriorating, his final string quartet showed anything but; the melodies remained young in a way that Haydn could not. His final work was inscribed with a quiet admission of Haydn’s weak physical state. 

Despite the devastating loss, he apparently accepted his fate with grace and humility.  He remained deeply respected across Europe, with visitors constantly coming to pay their respects. 

Franz Joseph Haydn passed away peacefully on May 31st of 1809 while Napoleon’s troops occupied Vienna. Even though the town he loved and cherished was racked with violence and fear, he played “Gott erhalte Franz den Kaiser” to comfort himself and those around him. Music, which had structured his entire life, became his final language. 

Conclusion 

Joseph Haydn’s final years were marked not by sudden tragedy, but by a gradual and deeply human surrender to time. Respected by the greatest musicians of the classical era, Haydn did not die a miserable old man. The composer died with a golden legacy, while remaining humble and candid through his works. Although Haydn was not immortal, his music certainly was, his earnest and beautiful music transcending time.

In 1977, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, abbreviated as NASA, sent out two identical golden discs into separate spacecrafts. Including instructions on how to play the records for whatever life may encounter, images of Earth and our location, the records also contained recordings of music of a plethora of varieties. Selected to be in the Voyager Golden Record was Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, arguably one of the greatest composers of all time. During his notoriously short life, he rapidly altered the music and composition that remain relevant in the modern day.  	


Childhood 

Symphony No. 1 in E-flat major


	Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born on January 27th of the year 1756 in the town of Salzburg, Austria. Mozart was one of two living children in his family, and he had a sister named Maria Anna Mozart. Similar to many other prolific composers, he was born into a family that was deeply interested in music, instilling a love for it into him at an early age. His father, a composer, and his mother, a talented singer, were vital in Mozart’s musical education, acting as his first teachers. 

By the time Mozart was five years old, he knew how to play numerous keyboard instruments, like the harpsichord and the organ, along with instruments of the stringed variety, like violin, viola, and cello. It is also worth noting that he was praised to have had a good singing voice. As he began to grow more proficient in music, he soon learned how to compose his own music, the earliest known piece being Köchel Verzeichnis 1. The minuet was written when he was five years old, which impressed his father. Moreover, the composer had perfect pitch, an excellent memory, and grew to be proficient in improvisation. Undoubtedly, these gave him a musical advantage that he would utilize to the fullest in adulthood. 

However, unlike other composers, his childhood was documented well due to his early rise to fame, catalyzed by Mozart’s father. Mozart’s father, Leopold Mozart, who was also renowned for his skill in composition and the violin, was able to recognize his children’s talent and formulated a plan to exploit it, which he enacted by touring his children, showcasing them. 

At the age of seven, Mozart and his sister, nicknamed Nannerl, were paraded around Austria and Germany. They were marketed as a pair of musical prodigies, gaining recognition from the aristocracy and royalty. In turn, the Mozart siblings were thrust into high society quickly. Undoubtedly, the sudden shift caused familial tension, particularly the dynamic between the father and son. It is believed that the Mozart family would earn the majority of their income through these extravagant tours, with Mozart being positioned as the “breadwinner.” This put an exorbitant amount of pressure on the young composer, as his father constantly pushed Mozart and his sister toward financial security. Leopold was one of his son’s greatest supporters, and at the same time, was portrayed as his opposition. As a child and as he transitioned into adolescence, he rebelled more frequently and more fiercely for his freedom, resentment bubbling between the two. 

While fame had its challenges, Mozart was fortunate in terms of the opportunities available to him. He had the chance to meet the famed composer,  J.S. Bach’s youngest son, Johann Christian Bach, during their tour where they stopped in England, when Mozart was only eight years old. While Mozart already had a steady foundation in music theory and composition, even as a child, his style was solidified by the son of the late-Baroque composer.
 
Soon after the first meeting, Johann Christian Bach, Mozart wrote their first symphony, Symphony No. 1 in E-flat major. Bach’s influence is evident in the changing composition style. The work was written during Mozart’s stay in the United Kingdom. It is said that it was written due to the fact that the Mozart siblings were not permitted to play the keyboard as their father recovered from an infection.  The symphony consists of three movements and is just over twelve minutes long. Although it is argued that the first symphony is neither one of Mozart’s lengthiest, nor amongst his most intricate works, it displays the immense potential that the composer possessed even as a young child. 


Adolescence 

Quaerite primum regnum Dei (K. 86).


When Mozart turned thirteen, and his sister eighteen, their paths diverged significantly. Maria Anna had reached adulthood and, due to societal gender norms, was forced to quit music and marry. This simultaneously promoted and encouraged Mozart. Mozart allegedly showed disdain at the decision; familial conflicts did not slow down Mozart’s own musical progression. In fact, he had only just begun. At the age of fourteen, Mozart was honored by Pope Clement XIV with a knighthood for his exceptional musical ability, as demonstrated by his remarkable transcription skills. Before this event, Mozart and his father, Leopold, travelled to Italy where Mozart studied as a composer. While Mozart had solidified his reputation as a capable and apt child prodigy, this is where he developed a personal style that combined wonderfully with his technical ability. Mozart was accepted into the Philharmonic Academy of Bologna with a religious choral piece called Quaerite primum regnum Dei (K. 86). The piece, split into four parts and written in D minor, was allegedly composed in less than half an hour, despite the limitations imposed on him. 
With the impressive composition, Mozart was accepted and admitted into the academy at the age of fourteen. This academy is where the young composer learned and refined advanced composition techniques, such as counterpoint, fugue composition, and improvisation, skills deemed vital for a young performer and writer to know. Whereas his ingenuity was recognized by critics across Europe, he was able to solidify his composing prowess under the tutelage of the academy. 


Early-Adulthood

Symphony No.31 in D major


Soon after transitioning into adulthood, Mozart would begin his journey in becoming an adult musician. The title of prodigy could not carry him beyond childhood as he sought work in Vienna as a composer or a musician. Mozart was eventually hired as a composer for Archbishop Colloredo in Salzburg. It is during this time under the employment of the Archbishop, that he began expanding on the music he composed, writing numerous piano and violin concertos, respectively. Coupled with his musical dissatisfaction, low pay, and encouragement from his father to seek a job elsewhere, Mozart was released from his musical obligations within the Archbishop’s court. This began his rampant search for work once more, looking all over Europe. Mozart toured around Europe, this time, not as a child prodigy, but as a musician seeking employment, only to come up empty handed in numerous major European cities. Accompanied by his mother, he travelled across the continent only for tragedy to strike. 

It was around this time when Mozart’s beloved mother became ill and died in 1777 while travelling with the composer. This was obviously devastating to him, and deeply affected his moral and relationship between his father and him, as Leopold resented the composer for the premature passing of his wife. It was during this jobhunt in Mannheim, in the year 1777, where he fell in love with Aloysia Webber, who too was born into a musical family. Aloysia was described to be a blossoming operatic singer, who took singing lessons from Mozart, who had been vocally trained in the Philharmonic Academy of Bologna. Mozart remained in Mannheim for about five months before returning the next year following the death of his mother. While it is said that the composer was still romantically interested in the singer, his advances were swiftly shut down by Aloysia, who, allegedly, viewed him as unimpressive. 

During this tumultuous time in the young composer’s life, he composed significant works, like his Piano Concerto in E-flat Major, and Symphony in D major. Consisting of three movements, spanning nearly twenty minutes, it is described to be energetic and fluttery, especially the first movement. This symphony is also frequently called “Paris” due to Mozart being in the namesake city during the composition process, weaving French-style preferences within the melody. Oftentimes, the Paris symphony is what many individuals believe is the peak of classical stylization. 

It was during this job hunt that Mozart, once more, was able to experience different classical stylistic genres from all over Europe that gave rise to his Paris symphony. Despite the immense pain he would have been under following the death of his mother, it can be said that his early-adulthood was the most colorful time of Mozart’s life, whether it adhered to the dark hues of grief, or the lighter shades of love. 


Golden Age 

The Marriage of Figaro: Voi che sapete (K.492, Act 2, Scene 4) 



Heartbroken after his numerous proposals of marriage were rejected by opera singer Aloysia Weber, Mozart’s eyes wandered and landed on Aloysia’s sister, Constanze Weber. The two met during the early 1780s when Mozart moved in. According to some sources, after being sexually intimate with one-another, they married, without the permission of Mozart’s father, to save themselves from public humiliation and scandal. Despite the nature and the conditions of their marriage, their union, made a few years later, was described to be sweet and romantic. On numerous occasions, when Mozart was performing abroad, he wrote affectionate and poetic letters to Constanze, showing how infatuated he was with his wife. In turn, this led to the composer and his wife conceiving children, the first of which, named Raimund Leopold, was born in 1783. However, the couple could not celebrate for long, as Raimund did not live to see his first birthday, due to the common infant mortality rates during Mozart’s era. 

Following the premature passing of his first-born son, both Mozart and his wife went through a sorrowful period of their lives. This painful process would repeat itself multiple times during the composer’s life, only two out of his six children living to adulthood, neither of them conceiving children. These losses heavily influenced his professional life outside of his family. It was during this time when he composed a vast amount of chamber music, like string quartets and piano sonatas that strengthened his reputation as a respectable and ingenious composer. 

In Vienna, Mozart sought noble patronage, respect, and official titles to secure his status and incomes, however, he was not able to satisfy these ambitions to the fullest, as he was famously terrible with money. Mozart’s income was unstable, and he was hyperdependent on commissions, teaching, and court appointments, as he did not hold permanent court positions. In addition to the uncertainty, Mozart was known to spend lavishly on extravagant and frivolous things, such as fancy clothes, friends, and socialization events, in an attempt to build connections with nobility. Along with the incurring cost of providing for his wife and children, he frequently borrowed money from those close to him. 

In spite of having the appearance of a successful musical artist, Mozart was deeply struggling, financially and emotionally. It was during this era, when his artistic success and creativity was precariously balanced against economic challenges, and his grief. In turn, he produced works of tremendous and ecstatic beauty. Written during the early and mid 1780s, after meeting Franz Joseph Haydn, affectionately named the father of the symphony, a series of string quartets were dedicated to Haydn and released. Haydn, in his middle ages, was reportedly fascinated with the comparatively young Mozart. In turn, the composer considered Haydn an admirable mentor, despite their differences, Mozart’s turbulence contrasting against Haydn’s calm nature. 

Although it is nearly impossible to single out Mozart’s best work from this era, amongst his most relevant and popular to this day is The Marriage of Figaro, an opera that he composed around 1786. The Marriage of Figaro was based on a play, and the composer had been commissioned to compose the comedic opera, injecting his genius through his ability to express various emotions into his pieces. It is within this opera that he writes Voi che sapete (K.492, Act 2, Scene 4), where a young boy sings of love and desire through a lyrical aria. It is with The Marriage of Figaro that Mozart was able to display his gift for blending character psychology with musical expression. 


Premature Passing 

Requiem 
	

Mozart’s relationship, like his father’s health, deteriorated during the late 1780s. Leopold was not only Mozart’s father first and foremost, he was a strict and rigorous teacher and manager. Many argue that if Leopold had not been so involved in his son’s musical career, Mozart would not have become as famous as he was, through harsh training, extenuating tours, and controlling schooling. This definitely caused strain, as Mozart grew older.

Leopold had been rapidly weakening, as he was suddenly unable to work, his reputation as a respected musician and teacher fading. Despite the complex bond the two had with one another, they inarguably cared for one another, Leopold worrying for his son’s financial future, and Mozart concerned for his father’s ailments. Nearly a decade after his wife, Leopold Mozart passed away, deeply affecting the composer. 

In the summer of 1791, Mozart received an anonymous commission for a Requiem Mass from an anonymous messenger representing Count Franz von Walsegg, whose wife had recently passed. However, Mozart was unaware of who had commissioned the piece, fueling rumors and fascination. Throughout 1791, he weakened while working on several projects, including the Requiem. 

One of the movements within the Requiem is the Lacrimosa in D minor, which Mozart composed eight bars for. The lyrics, sung in Latin, are based off of the Latin sequence known for its religious and grim meaning. Many of the lines speak of Jesus’s resurrection, rest, and rise, which was fitting for the piece that Mozart had been creating. The melody is hauntingly gorgeous, pensive, and poignant. It is reported that Mozart felt his own impending doom, and believed he was writing his own funeral music. Overall, the Requiem is gorgeous, showing off Mozart’s technical prowess, intended to be played by a large orchestra and sung by a choir of a similar magnitude.

The Requiem would be the last thing the composer would write before passing away at the age of thirty-six, leaving his wife Constanze behind on December 5th of 1791. While the cause of his death is debated, conspiracies alleging he was poisoned by his rival, Antonio Salieri, many historians disprove this theory and agree that Mozart died prematurely from either an infection or fever. Furthermore, numerous claim that Mozart died as a pauper, however, it is untrue. Mozart passed away leaving behind a modest estate, but leaving debt to his family. The Requiem was left unfinished and was only completed by Franz Xaver Sussmayr. It was performed posthumously. 


Conclusion 


Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s life could only be described as short but ecstatic. Like the man himself, his life was marked by grief, extraordinary love, beauty, and his otherworldly talent. Despite his devastatingly short existence, he is forever immortalized through his wondrous creations, one of them being preserved in golden records, drifting out into the horizon line. Mozart’s life proves that while life is finite, his memory is not.

In a time of limitless streaming and online playlists, something unexpected is happening in the music industry: vinyl records are outselling CDs. 2024 was the third consecutive year of the unexpected comeback, with 11 million more vinyl records sold than CDs.

Statistics show that this trend is only growing. Vinyl sales have been increasing for the last 18 years and have now reached $1.4 billion, the highest they’ve reached since 1984. But more surprisingly, collectors who grew up with vinyl aren’t the only ones behind this shift. Buyers aged 18 to 24 accounted for 18% of vinyl purchases in 2024, similar to the 20% from the 35 to 44 age group. Even though they have never experienced the format’s original peak, young people are among its most passionate buyers. 

But when millions of songs can fit into a pocket, why would people choose a more expensive and impractical option?

There's a variety of potential reasons, but one stands out in particular: vinyl takes up attention in ways that streaming can’t. Playing a record requires more effort than the click of a button; you must choose an album and place the needle. It doesn’t let you skip a song while scrolling through your phone or answering an email. Vinyl makes listening to music an experience rather than a background noise, which is rare in our fast-moving world. 

A vinyl is also something that you can physically hold. Although streaming is convenient, vinyl makes music feel like something that you own. Sound quality also plays a role, but not because it sounds objectively better. Vinyl has certain imperfections, such as crackles and slight distortions. It can make recordings feel more alive in contrast to the near-perfection of digital audio.

The rising popularity of vinyl doesn’t mean that people are rejecting technology. In fact, most vinyl collectors probably have music apps like Spotify. It means that more people want to slow down and actually appreciate what they’re listening to. By choosing vinyl, people are buying back their attention in a world where everything else is fighting for it.

Solis and Luna Arts (SLA) is a nonprofit organization that assists those with health issues through different art forms, primarily music. These student-led musical performances offer homage and comfort to those with medical concerns, which aligns with the definition of art therapy: a creative process utilized as a therapeutic and healing tool for individuals in need. Art and expression have been terms simultaneously intertwined with one another—as centuries ago and underscored today—they are seen as one. Art therapy is a celebration of the two similar traits into one. 

Art Therapy’s Historical Context

British artist Adrian Hill first created the formal practice and medical term of art therapy in 1942 in his published study on the benefits of art on individuals' minds. Hill personally discovered the therapeutic qualities of art when he battled tuberculosis in 1938, as he found that drawing and painting served as his creative outlet for his pain. After he recovered from tuberculosis and created the medical term art therapy, he became the first official art therapist in 1946 in the psychiatric hospital, Netherene, in the United Kingdom. 
Around the same time, Margaret Naumburg and Edith Kramer pioneered art therapy within the United States. Naumburg, a psychologist and educator, and Kramer, an artist utilized their expertise to spread awareness of art therapy and contribute their discoveries to the term. With more individuals becoming educated on the term and adding to the many discoveries between art and the cognitive mind, many associations such as The American Art Therapy Association founded in 1969, the Professional Association for Art Therapy in Australia, New Zealand, and Singapore in 1987 were created. 
Art therapy first helped individuals in the psychological healthcare demographic, which explains its spread to mental hospitals: because of the connection between painting and emotional release. Later, it was found to assist people not only mentally but also physically, proving itself a stimulating hobby for individuals experiencing a wide range of conditions. 

Art Therapy Today

Today, art therapy has evolved from its primary uses for psychological treatment to now being customizable and ever-changing depending on the practice and patient. The discoveries related to art therapy have also progressed, as art therapy today is a non-specific practice unrestricted to one age group; it is impactful for children and adolescents, adults, and the elderly. Additionally, art therapy not only aids individuals experiencing mental health struggles such as depression, anxiety, and PTSD by acting as an emotional outlet, but it also helps individuals going through medical issues. Specifically, art therapy has been found to assist adults suffering from hemodialysis, HIV/AIDS, Alzheimer's, and traumatic brain injuries. Since art therapy is so diverse and has different forms it can take on, it can be used to assist every demographic of people in need of any extra support.

Silent discos have gone from an experiment out of curiosity to a cultural phenomenon. At first, the concept almost feels surreal: just imagine a crowd of people dancing enthusiastically in a silent room. Once you put on the headphones, the whole idea makes perfect sense. It’s surprisingly social in a way traditional dance floors rarely are.

The origins of silent discos go back many decades, long before they became a recognizable feature at festivals and many nightlife events worldwide. Early versions were introduced as practical solutions to noise restrictions at outdoor gatherings. Instead of blasting speakers that disturbed nearby residents or wildlife, silent discos were noiseless as organizers shifted the sound directly into wireless headsets. The goal was to keep the music alive without creating any conflict. This invention brought something no one quite expected: that people actually enjoyed the experience for its own sake. 
 
What ultimately pushed silent discos into popularity was the unique level of control they give to each dancer. Instead of relying on a single DJ to ease into the mood of the entire night, attendees can choose the soundtrack that fits them best. Want to switch from house music to jazz halfway through a song? Just tap a button! The result is a dance floor that feels personalized and dynamic, offering space for different tastes without pulling people apart. Even if everyone is listening to something different, the shared environment brings a sense of connection that’s hard to describe until you’ve experienced it yourself.

Another key reason silent discos have spread so quickly is their flexibility. Because the music stays inside the headphones, these events can happen almost anywhere, such as rooftops, beaches, parks, community centers, and even libraries hosting late-night student events. Cities with strict noise regulations suddenly have a way to host vibrant gatherings without disrupting the whole neighborhood. As wireless audio technology improved, the experience became smoother, clearer, and more immersive. 

Silent discos have also expanded beyond nightlife as their popularity has grown. Big events like weddings use silent discos to keep guests dancing late without disturbing the venue. Another example is fitness instructors running silent yoga sessions where participants stay focused without outside noise. Even corporate events use them for workshops and team-building in shared spaces.

Silent discos are communal without being overwhelming and customizable without losing the excitement of a shared event. On another note, watching a crowd moving together to different beats while staying connected captures something uniquely modern about how we enjoy different types of music today!

Jazz, a genre of music that has captured the attention and minds of millions of people for over a century, had generational impacts on societies globally. To this day, jazz is listened to by 185 million people in the United States, constantly evolving and changing in new directions. But how did jazz achieve such a status? Where did jazz come from? How was jazz created?

The birth of jazz originates in the cultural melting pot of New Orleans, Louisiana, during the late 19th century. Jazz developed as a free-form, improvisational art form, influenced by a distinct fusion of American folk music, European harmonies, and African rhythms. It was born in the lively atmosphere of the city's dance halls, honky-tonks, and brothels, where musicians from diverse backgrounds came together to create new and unique pieces of music. Moreover, coming from West Africa and improvisations being the foundation of jazz, it was used as a form of self-expression for African Americans when their civil rights and native traditions were suppressed by racial segregation during that time.

Jazz's foundation was established by famous individuals who rose to prominence in the early 20th century. Jazz music's distinctive qualities were shaped by pioneers like virtuoso pianist and composer Jelly Roll Morton and Buddy Bolden, who is often regarded as the genre's founder.

In the 1920s, African Americans moved from the South to big cities like Chicago and New York, which greatly expanded jazz's appeal and ushered in the Jazz Age. Jazz reached its peak in popularity during this time, when it was dubbed the "Jazz Age." A wider audience was able to enjoy jazz thanks to the invention of the phonograph and radio. Prominent individuals such as Louis Armstrong, who is frequently referred to as the "father of jazz," transformed the practice of improvisation and made the trumpet's expressive potential well known. With the rise of big bands fronted by icons like Count Basie and Duke Ellington, jazz came to represent style, passion, and unrestrained freedom. 

As the 1930s progressed, the swing era gained prominence. Swing music, with its catchy rhythms and well-planned compositions, took over radio stations and dance floors. Jazz was further popularized by Benny Goodman, the "King of Swing," and Glenn Miller's orchestra, who became household names. Around the same time, vocalists like Ella Fitzgerald and Billie Holiday rose to fame, adding another dimension to the genre which was mostly instrumental prior.

With the introduction of bebop at the close of World War II, jazz underwent a dramatic transformation. Bebop, which was led by performers like Thelonious Monk, Dizzy Gillespie, and Charlie Parker, ignored the commercial limitations of swing in favor of improvisation, intricacy, and technique. Bebop's fast-paced and complex melodies required musicians to have a high level of technical skill, which introduced a new wave of jazz performers. Jazz evolved into a number of subgenres in the 1950s, each having distinct traits of its own. Cool jazz adopted a more laid-back and chill style, frequently fusing classical elements, under the direction of performers like Miles Davis and Dave Brubeck. Bebop was also enhanced with rhythm and blues elements by hard bop, which was promoted by musicians like Art Blakey and Horace Silver, resulting in a more approachable style of jazz.

The arrival of free jazz in the 1960s marked a significant break from conventional jazz norms. Free jazz, which was invented by performers like Ornette Coleman and John Coltrane, got rid of strict frameworks to allow for unrestricted improvisation and experimentation. At the same time, the fusion movement emerged, fusing jazz with electronic, rock, and funk components. A key figure in this fusion revolution was Miles Davis, whose albums included such as "Bitches Brew." 

Jazz is constantly evolving as we enter the modern period and absorbing elements from other genres. The expanding jazz landscape has benefited greatly from the contributions of Latin jazz, smooth jazz, and fusion. Jazz’s growth is carried on by modern performers like Wynton Marsalis, Esperanza Spalding, and Herbie Hancock, who continuously create music that makes the genre alive and well in the twenty-first century. 

We can see jazz's impact on schools as well, influencing music education and fostering a culture of creativity. Jazz education programs have emerged in schools worldwide, introducing students to the improvisational nature of the genre. Even in BCA, students like Alvin Li can join the school jazz band to delve more deeper into this category of music.

In his 2020 article “St. Patrick’s Day: The Tune,” Liam O’Connor explores the remarkable history and cultural journey of one of Ireland’s most recognizable melodies. Published by the Irish Traditional Music Archive, the piece traces the tune’s origins, development, and influence across centuries of Irish and global history. O’Connor shows how “St. Patrick’s Day” functions as more than just a piece of music. It is also a reflection of Irish identity, pride, and resilience that continues to resonate with people worldwide (O’Connor, 2020).

O’Connor begins by describing the tune’s uncertain origins. Often described as a 6/8 march or jig, “St. Patrick’s Day” first appeared in print in James Oswald’s The Caledonian Pocket Companion in the late 1750s. That collection featured both a 4/4 and a 6/8 version of the melody, showing how adaptable it was from the beginning (O’Connor, 2020). Edward Bunting later transcribed the tune from the harper Patrick Quinn in 1792 and published it in 1840, noting that the composer was unknown. Through these early examples, O’Connor illustrates the long and fluid history of the melody and its ability to evolve through both oral and written traditions.
The article also highlights how the tune became a central part of Irish dance culture. O’Connor references an account from 1936, when collector Nicolás Breathnach recorded a dancer from County Waterford who described tracing the shape of a shamrock with his steps to “St. Patrick’s Day.” This story shows how music and movement are intertwined to express Irish cultural identity. Dancing to the melody became both an art form and an act of cultural pride. By preserving and performing this tune, generations of Irish dancers reinforced shared traditions and connected music with national symbolism (O’Connor, 2020).

Beyond Ireland, O’Connor explores how “St. Patrick’s Day” accompanied Irish emigrants and became a reminder of home. He recounts a story from Rotha Mór an tSaoil by Micí Mac Gabhann, who heard the tune played by a piper in the Klondike goldfields of Canada. The sound moved him deeply, evoking powerful memories of his own homeland. Yet the same tune could also provoke division. In the same town, an “Orangeman” reacted angrily to the piper’s performance, leading to a violent confrontation (O’Connor, 2020). These contrasting reactions show how the melody symbolized unity and conflict alike, depending on who heard it and what it represented to them.

Finally, O’Connor shows that “St. Patrick’s Day” reached far beyond Irish communities. The tune inspired European composers such as Niccolò Paganini, who performed it with his own variations in 1831, and Beethoven, who arranged it orchestrally. Soldiers played and danced to it during wars, and it was even used to calm tensions between British troops and Zulu warriors. For some, it served as an unofficial national anthem; for others, it was simply a cheerful dance tune. Through these examples, O’Connor demonstrates the song’s lasting versatility and influence (O’Connor, 2020).

In “St. Patrick’s Day: The Tune,” O’Connor successfully captures how one melody embodies the Irish spirit through centuries of change. By blending historical detail, folklore, and musicology, he shows that “St. Patrick’s Day” is more than a familiar tune. It is a living part of Ireland’s cultural memory that continues to inspire joy, nostalgia, and connection across the world.

Music has been an integral part of human culture for nearly as long as humans have existed, serving as a universal language that brings people together. It has the extraordinary ability to evoke emotions, form shared experiences, and foster social connections. One of the primary ways music facilitates social connections is through shared experiences. When people attend a concert or music festival, they not only appreciate the performance but also participate in a collective experience. Concertgoers often find themselves singing along, dancing, and connecting with strangers in ways they would rarely do in other settings. The crowd’s shared emotions create a sense of unity and belonging. 
Music also plays a significant role in cultural celebrations and traditions by acting as a means of preserving heritage. Ranging from traditional folk songs to religious ceremonies, music is deeply intertwined with cultural identities. Shared musical experiences strengthen the bonds within communities, promoting a sense of belonging. They serve as connections to one's roots and a way to honor and pass down cultural values to future generations. Moreover, music is able to bridge cultural divides and develop understanding between diverse groups of people. Music festivals and concerts featuring artists from various backgrounds offer opportunities for audiences to appreciate and connect with different musical styles. This exposure allows individuals to develop deeper appreciation for cultural diversity and form bonds. 
Furthermore, the collaborative act of creating music can be a powerful catalyst for social bonding and connections. From singing in a choir or playing in a band to participating in informal sessions, shared musical experiences require cooperation, communication, and synchronization among participants. This combined effort cultivates trust, empathy, and a sense of shared accomplishment, strengthening the bonds between those involved. Additionally, the process of making music together can lead to deeper conversations and the sharing of personal experiences, further deepening the connections formed.
Music can also play a significant role in the formation of subcultures and communities centered around specific genres or artists. Fans of particular music styles often form tightly-knit groups, united by their shared passion and sense of belonging. Social media and online platforms have amplified these connections, allowing fans to connect, discuss, and share their love for music across the world in virtual communities that extend beyond physical limitations.
Ultimately, music's power to bring people together and foster social connections is undeniable. Whether through shared experiences at concerts, preserving cultural heritage, bridging cultural divides, collaborative music-making, or forming subcultures, music serves as a universal language that creates a sense of unity and belonging. By harnessing the emotional and communal aspects of music, individuals can forge lasting bonds and deepen their understanding of one another, making music an invaluable aspect of human experience and culture.

Paul Simon and Art Garfunkel, a duo famously known as “Simon & Garfunkel”, made a major mark on 20th-century music. They emerged from the 1960s folk revival, blending rich acoustics, harmonies, and poetic lyrics that shaped popular music for years. Even though the pair’s time together was brief, their influence still shows up in the work of many musicians across different genres.

Simon & Garfunkel stood out because they mixed depth with simplicity. Early songs like Scarborough Fair and The Sound of Silence captured the thoughtful mood of a generation facing rapid change. Unlike some of their peers who wrote direct, confrontational songs of protest, their approach was more thoughtful and philosophical. Their use of intricate melodies and subtle lyrics inspired pop and rock artists to express complex feelings without sounding sentimental or aggressive. Artists like James Taylor, Joni Mitchell, and Phoebe Bridgers have all named this style as a key influence.

The duo’s innovative use of studio production is another aspect of their legacy. They collaborated with their producer, Roy Halee, to develop innovative methods that tore through the traditional bounds of folk music. The acoustic genre reached symphonic heights thanks to the layered vocal arrangements on songs like The Boxer and the dynamic changes in Bridge Over Troubled Water. For later musicians like Fleetwood Mac, Bon Iver, a new playing field was set by these recordings, which showed that folk music could be both grand and intimate. Paul Simon extended this experimental style in his solo album Graceland, combining South African motives with pop and rock before cross-cultural music became popular.
​
Just as notably, Simon & Garfunkel transformed the definition of a musical duo. Garfunkel's melodious voice and Simon's analytical, thoughtful songwriting combined to create an unmatched synergy, forming a balance between individuality and collaboration. From the lyricist-composer relationship between Elton John and Bernie Taupin to the minimalist duos of indie music today, this dynamic has sparked generations of collaborations. They demonstrated that musical chemistry could be just as potent as lyrical content by using harmonic themes to evoke strong emotional resonance.

Their music became inextricably linked to the culture of the 1960s and early 1970s. Songs like America and Mrs. Robinson, which balanced social criticism with introspection, encapsulated both the period's optimism and disillusionment. Simon & Garfunkel also contributed to the understanding of how music could influence cinematic storytelling by appearing in classic movies like The Graduate. Not only did their songs accompany and enhance scenes, but they also gave them deeper meanings and subcontexts that revolutionized the connection between music and film. This method opened the door for later incorporation of popular music in movies, influencing filmmakers, whose works frequently use well-selected soundtracks to evoke emotion and paint a fuller picture.

Simon & Garfunkel's legacy endures because they harnessed the power of musical diversity to its fullest and incorporated elements from all parts of the creative world: folk tradition, contemporary experimentation, simplicity, sophistication, and the human experience. Their brief but effective partnership showed that popular music could be deeply human, poetic, and artistic. Their sound continues to inspire musicians who are looking for integrity, beauty, and purpose in their work, even decades after their breakup. The lasting impact of Simon & Garfunkel's work serves as a reminder that, in a society which frequently values loudness and spectacle, depth, harmony, and personal connection make the strongest statements.

You likely know a hit song of the 5-time Grammy winner Childish Gambino: This is America, Redbone, 3005, Heartbeat, Sober… Childish Gambino’s music is characterized by its versatility and thought-provoking lyrics. Rather than sticking to one genre, he blends rap, R&B, soul, and psychedelic rock. Like his music, Gambino’s talent spans multiple fields—comedy, writing, directing, singing, and rapping. Thus, his real name, Donald Glover, is as well known as his stage name.

Glover was born on September 25, 1983, and grew up in Stone Mountain, Georgia. After graduating from New York University’s Tisch School of the Arts in 2006, he broke into the entertainment industry when Tina Fey hired him to write for and act in the sitcom 30 Rock. He rose to fame through his role as Troy Barnes in four seasons of the comedy sitcom Community. 

Glover then gained momentum as he developed and starred in his own show, Atlanta. This comedy tells the story of an up-and-coming rapper, Alfred Miles, whose career is managed by his cousin, Earn Marks, played by Glover. Praised for brilliant artistry, surreal portrayal of hip-hop culture, and authentic portrayal of the Black experience in America, the show was nominated 26 times for the Emmys and won twice. 

At the same time, Glover released his first album, “Camp,” in 2011. He also adopted the stage name “Childish Gambino,” which was generated randomly from a Wu-Tang Clan name generator. The album received mixed reviews for using a lighthearted “punchline rap” style to portray serious issues like race and masculinity, as well as for the sense that he was imitating other rappers like Drake and Kanye West. However, others praised his rapping skills and catchy tunes.

The release of “Because of the Internet” in 2013 turned Glover’s music career around. He launched an ambitious multimedia campaign around the release of this album, including a short movie titled Clapping for the Wrong Reasons and a 76-page, four-act screenplay. The album follows the story of “the Boy” as he spirals into an existential crisis while reflecting upon his rich but lonely life. Before this album’s release, Glover was sometimes viewed as a comedian or TV actor dabbling in rap; afterwards, he was treated as a serious artist.

In 2016, Glover released his third album, “Awaken, My Love!” In contrast to the heavy rap and wordplay in his previous two albums, the dreamy vibes and exploration of soul and psychedelic rock were more prominent. Concurrently, Glover climbed higher in the acting industry, playing Lando Calrissian in Solo: A Star Wars Story and Aaron Davis in Spider-Man: Homecoming. 

Donald Glover’s fame has only grown since then. In 2022, he was announced to star in and produce a feature set in a Spider-Man movie. In 2023, he became a head writer of the Star Wars series Lando. He recently released his studio albums “Atavista” and “Bando Stone & the New World” in 2024. However, Glover suffered a stroke in October 2024 during his “The New World Tour,” forcing him to cancel the remaining shows. 

Spanning over 20 years, Donald Glover’s career has brought him fame in multiple fields. He has left lasting impressions as a musical artist, comedian, actor, and director. His unique versatility and ability to excel in many roles at once showcase the capabilities of his talent.
