Attending a Solis and Luna music concert, you’ll see the eyes of the senior home patients light up as they engage themselves in music they are familiar with. You will see high school musicians on the stage, who have little in common with their audience. Intergenerational gaps can almost feel like speaking a different language, but with music as a bridge and a universal language, people of diverse backgrounds can instantly connect. As age-associated diseases like dementia become more common in our society and the younger generations are becoming more isolated by social media, we must take advantage of music’s ability to heal, sustain health, and create connections. 

Performing at a Solis and Luna Arts concert is a fun and relaxing experience for our high school musicians and is an uplifting experience for the audience. How can both the performers and the audience benefit from music? Music is scientifically shown to release the hormones dopamine, associated with “chills,” serotonin, often related to positive moods, and oxytocin, known for boosting social bonding and regulating stress. The release of these hormones is equally critical for senior patients and high school musicians and can ease their bonding experience. Senior patients who may feel lonely and isolated or who may suffer from dementia naturally feel more sociable and cheerful. Similarly, high schoolers who feel isolated due to social media and stress from school can unwind and form genuine connections by playing music together. 

In fact, music as a form of connection across generations is almost instinctual: New York Times Author and grandmother Paula Span notes that she bonded with her grandchildren through singing to them, an action that is repeated in many cultures. Generally, people feel a sense of belonging and togetherness when they share something in common with another person. It is also fascinating to see intergenerational collaborations in the music field: Paul Simon, singer and guitarist from Simon & Garfunkel, and Sabrina Carpenter, a rising pop star, recently collaborated to sing “Homeward Bound.” They are 58 years apart, but Paul’s maturity and Sabrina’s youth create a captivating blend. Making music across generations isn’t just an act of collaboration, but also highlights the harmonizing beauties of youth and maturity. 

Music has the power to tell captivating stories that transcend generations and boundaries, and leveraging this power can unite generations, boost moods, and create new bonds.

Hailey Tsai is the Region Director of the Solis and Luna Arts Manhattan County Art region, which hosted its first event at the senior living center Sunrise at East 56th. Throughout the event, Tsai ensured that the seniors were engaged and focused on the process rather than the product. With neurographic art, Solis and Luna Arts members were able to talk to the seniors and bring calm and joy to the room.

Q: What initially inspired you to join SLA and pursue art therapy with seniors?

A: I’ve always been interested in mental health and art, especially the intersection between the two. When I learned that SLA was incorporating art therapy into its programming, I immediately thought it was something really special. I was excited by the idea of using creativity as a way to support seniors and build meaningful connections. I’ve also seen firsthand how powerful art therapy can be for people, which made me even more motivated to get involved and help grow the program.

Q: What prior experiences shaped your approach to volunteering here?

A: I’ve volunteered for several years at my taekwondo school, where we emphasize not only physical training but also the mental aspect. Although I worked mostly with younger children, the experience taught me how to work with others, teach patiently, and communicate with intention. I helped teach taekwondo forms and kicks, led arts and crafts activities, and explained the values behind the practice—discipline, perseverance, self-control, and respect. That experience shaped how I approach volunteering now, especially in understanding that teaching and connection go beyond just the activity itself.

Q: What are your favorite art mediums to use?

A: My favorite mediums are watercolor and gouache. That said, I was surprised by how much I enjoyed using markers and colored pencils during our first sessions in Bergen County and Manhattan. I’d also love to try oil painting someday and continue exploring new materials.
Q: What inspires you to create art? Tell me about your journey in art-making.

A: For a long time, I mostly created art for other people—birthday gifts, school assignments, etc. I didn’t really make art just for myself. I started drawing more consistently in middle school, especially during COVID, but when I entered high school and took ceramics, I struggled to bring myself to paint or draw in my free time. I felt stuck creatively. 

That changed last summer when I participated in an art residency program through my school. We were completely immersed in nature and lived without our devices for a week. For the first time, I created art purely for myself. I explored different mediums, discovered that I enjoy working with gouache the most, tried charcoal for the first time, and realized that I now love painting portraits more than landscapes, which surprised me. That experience taught me so much about myself as an artist and helped me let go of expectations. My goal became simply to create art I wanted to make, without constraints or pressure.

Q: Can you describe a moment or any changes you observed where art-making positively affected a participant’s mood, social connection, communication, or confidence?

A: One participant I worked with was very quiet at the beginning of the session. During a neurographic art exercise, she began adding more free-form lines, circles, and colors that reflected her emotions. As the piece developed, her energy noticeably shifted. By the end, she shared that she felt relaxed and proud of her work, which was really meaningful to witness.

Q: Can you share an interaction that left a meaningful impact on you? 

A: One participant was no longer able to physically grip a marker, so instead, he shared his ideas, emotions, and color choices with me. He talked through what he wanted to express on the page, and I tried my best to translate his thoughts into the artwork. That interaction reminded me that art is about expression and communication, not just the physical act of creating, and it changed how I think about accessibility in art.

Q: What skills have you developed through this work? 

A: Through this experience, I’ve really developed my ability to work with others more thoughtfully. I’ve learned how to listen closely, adapt to different needs, and communicate with patience and empathy.

Q: If you could change or improve one thing about the program, what would it be? 

A: Right now, I wouldn’t change anything. In the future, though, it could be exciting to explore additional forms of therapeutic art beyond neurographic art and continue expanding the program’s creative possibilities. 

Q: What was your favorite part about conducting the program?

A: My favorite part was working with others and getting to know the participants—their stories, their emotions, and how they experienced the art-making process.

Q: What advice would you give to people wanting to get involved with therapeutic arts?

A: I would encourage people to reach out, build connections, and really reflect on why they want to get involved. I would say think about how you can make an impact, stay open to learning from others, and remember that even small moments of connection can be incredibly meaningful.

In an insightful interview with Ms. Jee-Hoon Krska, the founder of Keys 2 Success, we explored how Solis and Luna and Keys 2 Success work in harmony to bring the joy of music to different communities. Tune in to our podcast to hear Chloe and Ms. Krska’s full discussion! 

W warmly welcomed Ms. Krska to tell the story of her nonprofit organization, Keys 2 Success. As an MIT graduate and Juilliard Pre-College-trained pianist, she shares her passion for music with underserved communities in Newark, New Jersey. When asked to explain the impetus behind founding Keys 2 Success, she said: “America is a land of opportunity, but is not a land of opportunity for everyone. Unfortunately, it's not a land of opportunity for a lot of people who have been in America for generations, namely African Americans.” Ms. Krska started her journey teaching two students in a small closet and now has over 200 students across Newark’s five wards. owns 

	Chloe then asked Ms. Krska to share an impactful moment about Keys 2 Success, to which she responded that she is constantly learning the meaning of community. Ms. Krska observed that many people who grew up in the suburbs don’t realize that life is somewhat isolating; people are limited to their backyards and neighbors don’t often converse. However, neighborhoods in Newark feel like one big family, which has taught Ms. Krska important values throughout the years of working with students from Newark. She brings the feeling of a tight-knit community to music by encouraging students to learn together and help one another. Chloe added on with a similar experience at Solis and Luna. She noted that oftentimes, music organizations perform complex classical pieces for senior center patients which they cannot fully appreciate. However, by arranging popular oldies like “Can’t Help Falling in Love” by Elvis Presley, the audience can reminisce about their past and connect with the musicians. Despite the intergenerational difference, our musicians easily bond with their audiences through their shared love of music. For Chloe and Ms. Krska, music is a uniting factor that brings together different people. 

	Lastly, Chloe and Ms. Krska talked about what music means to them. Ms. Krska explained that music is one thing she can control amidst many uncontrollable elements in life. For example, as a teenager, she did not have power over which colleges accepted her, but she could always shape a phrase until it was exactly how she liked. Therefore Ms. Krska asserted that “not giving students the gift of music is a little bit of a crime.” Chloe felt similarly and added on, emphasizing her appreciation for enriching school music classes which she always looked forward to.  

	All in all, Chloe and Ms. Krska’s different experiences with music intertwine harmoniously to show just how impactful music can be. They first met through Vivian, the Essex County Region Director, who works with both organizations. However, this will certainly not be the last collaboration between Solis and Luna and Keys 2 Success. Stay tuned to see what the future holds!

What started as doodles in childhood and hours of sketching during the pandemic has now grown into leadership in the field of creative arts. Today, we’ll hear how Bergen Tech senior Hailey Shen turned her creative outlet into a way to help others express themselves, heal, and connect through art.

Hailey Shen is a current senior at Bergen Tech in the Digital Media program. She is also the Art Therapy Region Director for Bergen County and the first-ever Art Therapy Region Director at Solis and Luna Arts. Her introduction of the power of visual arts to Solis & Luna has also encouraged the inclusion of other creative arts therapies. Today, we’ll hear more about her inspiring journey as an artist, applying art therapy in her life, and how she became an art therapy regional director!

Hailey has always been drawn to art throughout her life, drawing ever since she was young, then going on to take art more seriously during the COVID-19 pandemic. She began painting and using other art mediums at Bergen Tech, where she’s been able to add digital media, acrylic painting, graphite, and many other skills to her artistry. Hailey also enjoys experimenting with materials like plexiglass and has even created a whole piece using a single ballpoint pen. 

As Hailey reflects on her artwork, she realizes how art has been a meaningful way of documenting her life, inner thoughts, and growth in a physical way. “Art is a really good form of self-expression,” Hailey said in the Spotlight Series podcast interview, “It can act as just like a creative outlet, or a form of art therapy and emotional relief.”

Hailey first brought up the possibilities of incorporating visual arts into Solis and Luna Arts at a meeting with Chloey, Solis & Luna’s founder, where they discussed the idea of more creative art therapies. Hailey is now our first visual arts therapy region director in Bergen County, where she recently held her first event at Brookdale Emerson. She did research beforehand on art therapy techniques, then outlined a plan to best create neurographic art with the senior citizens. Neurographic art involves drawing abstract, free-flowing lines, and afterwards rounding out the sharp edges. It is meant as a way for people to get out their frustration and other emotions on paper. Hailey recalls watching the senior citizens enjoy the activity, connect over their experiences with the SLA members, both verbally and non-verbally. She’s excited to continue reaching wider audiences with more members and art therapy techniques.

Becoming a region director, especially for something as exacting as art therapy, can be daunting for young people. Hailey, however, has taken it in stride with an organized and collaborative approach. She admits the hardest part is just starting, and oftentimes, though it may sound cliché, the value is all in the process and journey. Hailey coordinates well with her team members and the senior center, makes sure to do her research on proper techniques for the art therapy session, and later reflects on what worked (and didn’t) in the session to ensure improvements and meaningful impact for future sessions. She encourages others to get involved with Solis, whether it be becoming an art therapy director, joining her writing team, or any of the other accessible opportunities we offer!

The Solis & Luna Arts Podcast recently featured an inspiring conversation with the string winners of the 2025 Solis & Luna Arts Autumn Music Competition, cellist Cade Wyles and violist Edward Lee. This episode offered listeners an in-depth look at the musicians behind the performances, highlighting not only their achievements but also their personal journeys, challenges, and values that continue to shape their artistry.

Cade Wyles, a 20-year-old sophomore at the Fredonia State College of Music, reflected on how his passion for the cello began at a young age. Having parents who were not musicians themselves, Cade found his earliest inspiration through recordings of Yo-Yo Ma, whose sound drew him to the cello’s expressive range and depth. After being told that he was too young to play the bass and settling for cello at age six, Cade steadily developed his craft, eventually earning the opportunity to perform as a soloist after winning the Buffalo Philharmonic Orchestra Youth Concerto Competition, an experience he described as especially meaningful due to the chance to share the stage with teachers and mentors who had shaped his musical path.

Edward Lee, an 18-year-old senior at Bergen County Academies and a Juilliard Pre-College student, spoke about the strong influence of his older sister on his musical development. He began studying music at age six as well, initially playing violin before switching to viola in elementary school. Edward explained that the viola’s tone resonated more deeply with him, a choice he has never regretted. He credited early studio classes and frequent performance opportunities with helping him develop confidence, consistency, and a sense of comfort on stage.

Both musicians emphasized how summer festivals and intensive programs played a pivotal role in their growth. Edward shared his experiences with the National Youth Orchestra and Morningside Music Bridge, describing these environments as both demanding and transformative. Cade resonated with these profoundly transformative experiences, noting that such programs helped him push past comparison and instead focus on personal progress, musical curiosity, and collaboration with peers from around the world.

The interview also explored the distinction between performing as a soloist and playing within an orchestra. Edward discussed the responsibility of leading musically while remaining deeply connected to the ensemble and sustaining a sense of balance, while Cade highlighted the heightened pressure, memorization, and stellar projection required of soloists. Both agreed that these experiences fostered greater musical awareness, confidence in oneself, and leadership.

Another central theme of the episode was balance. Specifically, managing rigorous academic responsibilities alongside intensive practice schedules. Cade and Edward spoke openly about time management, organization, and learning to set realistic expectations. They stressed the importance of fundamentals, noting that scales, etudes, and thoughtful warm-ups become increasingly essential over time, both for technical development and physical well-being.
Beyond technique and discipline, the musicians reflected on the importance of community in the classical music world. They emphasized that chamber music, orchestras, and festivals create lasting relationships that often extend far beyond a single performance or season. As both noted, the music world is remarkably small, and maintaining strong connections is often just as important as individual achievement.

Looking ahead, both musicians expressed a clear desire to keep music central in their futures. Edward hopes to continue pursuing orchestral and chamber music, building teamwork skills. Cade shared his plans to combine performance with music education, with aspirations of teaching in public school and, eventually, earning a master's degree to coach at the collegiate level.
In closing, Cade and Edward offered advice to younger musicians: be patient, trust the process, stay consistent with fundamentals, and take time to enjoy the people and experiences that music brings. Their conversation served as both a celebration of artistic excellence and a thoughtful reminder that growth in music is as much about connection, persistence, and kindness toward oneself as it is about performance.

Listeners can look forward to upcoming podcast episodes featuring the woodwind section winners of the 2025 Solis & Luna Arts Autumn Music Competition.

Solis & Luna arts is led by an incredible team of qualified individuals. One of these individuals is Victor Hsu. “Our vision includes the creation of multiple school clubs worldwide, enabling students from various regions to access the benefits of musical therapy.”

“Furthermore, we are actively seeking partnerships with additional organizations, building upon our existing collaboration with Make-A-Wish. Under the leadership of Victor and the rest of the board, Solis & Luna continues to grow and become more accessible for all to enjoy the benefits of music therapy. Everyday, Solis & Luna continues to spread the healing power of music to more and more people. The idea of helping others with their musical passion motivates those in the organization to keep on going, producing remarkable results and feelings of happiness for the community.

Over the years, Solis & Luna Arts has led hundreds of members worldwide in hosting music therapy concerts, bringing comfort and joy to thousands of patients. The nonprofit is now expanding beyond music therapy to embrace a larger spectrum of creative arts. 

Art is increasingly recognized as a meaningful way for individuals to express themselves and find joy. With the new visual art program, Solis & Luna Arts aims to utilize art-based activities as opportunities for companionship, connection, and creative engagement. By bringing teenagers together with senior citizens, the program allows for shared creativity and fosters inclusivity.

On August 17, 2025, Solis & Luna’s first art chapter, based in Bergen County, launched its program at Brooksdale Emerson, a senior living and patient care center. Led by Bergen County Art Director Hailey Shen, the team introduced neurographic art as a meditative activity that uses lines, curves, and shapes to reflect the flow of thoughts and emotions. Unlike traditional drawing, which often replicates a specific image, neurographic art encourages more organic and neuron-like patterns, offering participants a relaxing and creative experience.

The process begins with drawing a wandering line across the page. Seniors are encouraged to release emotions and frustration as they fill the paper. Frustration may appear in jagged marks, while calmness may show through soft, curved lines. Then, sharp intersections are softened by rounding them out. Each softened corner helps signal the nervous system to calm the brain. From there, the team encourages the seniors to experiment with new art mediums, vary line thickness, trace new shapes, and fill them with layers of color. 

Growing research highlights the potential benefits of engaging in the arts. Studies have shown that art-making can influence brain function and cognitive processes, supporting emotion regulation, stress reduction, and resilience. For example, a 2014 study conducted by Anne Bolwerk and colleagues examined the effects of visual art production and cognitive art evaluation on post-retirement adults. The study found that those who engaged in art-making demonstrated increased resilience and improvements in brain connectivity, suggesting that creative activities can play a valuable role in overall well-being.

Solis & Luna Arts is excited to continue bringing people together through music, art, and shared creativity! The organization plans to launch more creative art programs, including but not limited to nail therapy, floral therapy, and fashion therapy.

I’m sure many of you reading this blog can agree that music is a significant part of our lives. While I'm sure most of us enjoy listening to music, many of us don’t truly and fully understand the amazing effects that music has on our health: Music can help our physical and mental health and wellbeing! Through treatments like musical therapy, people can achieve their goals. Music therapy is a lesser known type of treatment, and while the field seems somewhat vague, there are actually 4 specific types of music therapy: compositional, improvisation, receptive, and re-creative music therapy. 

First, compositional music therapy involves a therapist guiding clients in creating their own music. With this guidance, a songwriter can unleash creativity, show vulnerability by sharing emotions and experiences, get past musicians' block and feel validation in their skills and capabilities. 

Next, there is receptive music therapy, this type of therapy encourages clients to listen to music and respond to it. This response could be through art, dance, silence, or speech. Here, music could be used with imagery, to possibly stimulate relaxation and reduce anxiety. Using this can not only enrich listening skills, but also help one explore their memories, trauma, or grief to find closure. 

Additionally, when using music recreation therapy, the client plays or sings along to new or familiar music.people can achieve their goals, improve their skills, use music as a coping mechanism and express themselves. 

Finally, improvisation therapy consists of making spontaneous music. Therapists are able to interpret the client's mood based on this musical expression. Through this intervention, people can focus on expression through music, take creative liberty and build relationships through making music. 

Music therapy isn't very renowned or commercialized, it has yet to reach a zenith of recognition in terms of helping clients achieve their goals. The stats speak for themselves: with the implementation of music theory improve anxiety levels and depressive symptoms by significant amounts. Additionally, Music therapy has been shown to reduce heart rate in adult critical-care patients by an average of 7 beats per minute. Even music therapy can increase social interaction in children with disabilities by 38% There are so many other mind blowing statistics as well that you can explore here: https://gitnux.org/music-therapy-statistics/

It is important to keep in mind that these professionals are very qualified considering that over 95% of them have a degree in Music Therapy or related fields, and there are almost 5,000 board certified music therapists. 

So what can we do to improve the music therapy industry? For starters, we can educate more of the public on the importance of music therapy. We could also work on funding for research and narrowing down specific ways it could be used. Additionally, we could utilize more of music therapy in healthcare settings like hospitals, rehabilitation and mental health centers, the practice can be incorporated alongside recovery plans. With more public funding for music therapists and insurance coverage for the practice, we can remove financial hurdles and make music therapy more accessible to everyone

Ludwig van Beethoven
(1732-1809)
	
In an era of AI-generated music, controversial discussions about art, and who has the talent or potential to create with the assistance of bots, Ludwig van Beethoven is a frequent name mentioned in the debates. Ludwig van Beethoven was a prolific composer known for an immaculate bridge between the classical and romantic genres that remain recognizable today, his passion for music and the arts that transcended beyond his era, life, senses, and, towards the end of his life, his disability. Also, being the initiator of the “Curse of the Ninth”, the composer serves as the perfect example of how passion surpasses all.


Childhood 

Nine Variations on a March by Dressler for piano in C minor
	

Not many can find a connection between the theme of classical music and a beet farm. However, a plethora of classical music fanatics’ minds will immediately jump to Beethoven, whose family name means “from the beet farm”. The late classical composer was born in Bonn, Germany, in December 1770. His exact birthdate is unknown.

Despite their namesake, the Beethoven family was not farmers; they were musicians. Moreover, his father, Johann von Beethoven, was very involved in the young composer’s musical education, teaching Beethoven musical theory and how to play various instruments at a young age. A vital thing to note is that Beethoven was born nearly fifteen years after the rise of the young Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, who had toured around Europe among royalty as a prodigious budding musician. It can be assumed that perhaps Johann, seeing the explosive success of Mozart’s musical tour, wanted his son to follow in his footsteps and become a well-known prodigy himself. Furthermore, many speculate that the fierce advocacy for his son’s success in his musical career can be attributed to Johann’s lack of which in his own. This is why Johann started to weave musicality and technique into the young composer’s life, starting from when he was a child. 

However, Beethoven’s childhood unfortunately came to greatly resemble Mozart’s, taking a violent and abusive turn. In Johann’s impatient desire to create a musical spectacle, he frequently became violent with his son over menial mistakes, causing physical altercations with the young composer, forcing his son into long practice sessions, and withholding fatherly affection that greatly impacted their dynamic. Apparently, the violence escalated to Beethoven’s father shutting him into a cellar while under the influence of alcohol. Furthermore, according to the same source, Thayer’s Life of Beethoven, “... this young Ludwig was compelled, sometimes, no doubt, through the fear or the actual infliction of punishment for neglect; sometimes, too, the father, whose habits were to as to favor a bad interpretation of his conduct, was no doubt harsh and unjust.” This insinuates that the early passion Beethoven displayed for the arts came from his father’s overbearing dominance. From attempting to replicate the genius and the success generated by Mozart, the composer’s father unfortunately created the same resentment that Mozart felt for his father in young Beethoven.

Once more, this caused Beethoven to adore his mother much more than his father, a natural consequence of having a strict and abusive paternal figure. Yet, it is evident that the abuse and neglect were present on both sides, of varying degrees, as the disturbing conditions continued without intervention from either parent. As to why his precious mother never stopped the abuse is unknown and speculated on, some wondering whether she too was involved in the terrifying childhood that Beethoven was forced to live through. Regardless of the lack of interference, Beethoven cherished his mother. 

Despite the tumultuous and harsh relationship between father and son, Johann’s desire to raise a prodigy was realized as Beethoven’s talent flourished in many instruments. Before the composer had turned a decade old, he knew how to play various keyboard instruments, the violin, and the viola, in the hopes that he would become a musician like his family members. While his musical education was expedited and prioritized, his academic studies were comparably ignored, claiming that his grammar and mathematics skills were deficient compared to those of his age. The young Beethoven debuted to the public at seven years old. Allegedly, according to various sources, he was advertised to have been six years old when he was, in fact, one year older. The reasons for that are speculated to be that Beethoven’s father wanted to draw comparisons between his son and the famed Mozart. The sudden attention must have been a lot for Beethoven, as he was frequently described as a quiet and shy young boy. 

A year away from turning ten, Beethoven had officially surpassed the level of his father, necessitating a new teacher. Johann hired multiple teachers before settling on Van den Eeden, who taught Beethoven organ technique in the style of other Baroque-Classical composers like Handel and Bach. However, most prominently, he was studying composition and the organ under the tutelage of Christian Gottlob Neefe, whom Beethoven spoke of fondly during the later years of his life, and it is not a surprise that he looked at his old master so favorably, despite the criticism given to the young composer regarding his composition and progress. Although he would come to study with one of the greatest classical composers and musicians of his era, he always credits Neefe for his early influence on his composition. It was Neefe who assisted Beethoven in releasing his first major work, the Nine Variations on a March by Dressler for piano in C minor. It was published in the early 1780s, when he was about twelve years old. While there were likely more compositional pieces that were written before this publication, it was his first official piece. The variations were named as such based on the original march written by Dressler. This is far from the most impressive work produced by Beethoven, but it sets up the compositional foundation necessary for him to produce the magnificent pieces he is well-known for today. 


Adolescence 
Piano Concerto No.2 in B-flat major, Op.19


	At twelve years old, with the assistance of teachers, the young composer was offered the position of cembalist in an orchestra, a harpsichord or pianoforte player. At this point, Beethoven was impressing those left and right with his ability to sightread and with his refined technique. At the age of fourteen, he was employed as an assistant court organist, beginning to compose various pieces and branching out. While Beethoven was slowly improving technically in both musicality and composition, his familial financial situation was resting on his shoulders, which could have placed an immense burden on him. At this point, his father was so inebriated and unable to support the family by himself that he put the responsibility on his adolescent son’s shoulders. It was during this time that he wrote three piano quartets. Written for four instruments, piano, violin, viola, and cello, he wrote them in various keys. While Beethoven is infamous for his romantic expression in his later years, the pieces written throughout his adolescence adhere to the classical style set by his compositional predecessors, like Haydn, whom he would come to study with in the future. 

	While the early 1780s were considered pivotal in his artistic and personal life, the late 1780s would be more so, as he travelled to Vienna. It was here that he was likely met or in the presence of Mozart, after whom his father modelled his son’s musical training. It is debated heavily whether the two personally met, but many historical scholars agree that Mozart, at least, praised Beethoven as having great potential and to keep an eye out for him and his work in the future. 

	However, the ecstasy that took hold of Beethoven’s heart upon receiving praise from his idol was quickly stolen away by the premature demise of his mother, whom he loved dearly. Beethoven’s mother, Maria Magdalena Beethoven, passed away from a tuberculosis infection. The teenage composer had returned from Vienna to his hometown, Bonn, to stay with her before she passed away. In quick succession, his youngest sibling also lost her life. Beethoven’s familial life was marked with tragedy, his mother passing away at only forty years old, and five of his seven siblings and half-siblings dying in infancy. Despite infant death being common in the era, due to the rudimentary medical treatments and dangerous practices, these losses took a heavy emotional toll on the young Beethoven. 	

	As his mother was the one to financially manage the family, the Beethoven’s responsibilities would only grow exponentially as he would live with his alcoholic father and the remainder of his living siblings. The consecutive deaths of his mother and youngest sister ended any prospects of studying in Vienna with Mozart. It was amidst this tragic era of Beethoven’s life that he was working on his Piano Concerto No.2  in B-flat major, Op.19, but it was not performed nor finished until 1795, when Beethoven was twenty-five years old. Evidently from the era, the piece leans more towards a classical stylization that Beethoven would come to blend with the romantic genre in his later years. At this period in his life, he was still trying to find his signature style and was a chameleon to different ones, his piano concerto resembling Mozart’s works. Despite the piece being considered one of his earlier works, it displays the wield that Beethoven had in terms of musicality and technical prowess. 


Early Adulthood

Piano Trio No.3 in C minor (Op.1, No.3)


	Following Beethoven’s legal succession in becoming the head of the household, he began his transition from childhood to adulthood. Beethoven was able to financially support his brothers and father through playing viola in an orchestra. In the early 1790s, Beethoven would find his footing and would move to Vienna, largely considered the music capital of Europe, to study with Franz Joseph Haydn. In his mid-twenties, while Haydn was on his way to London, he met the blossoming Beethoven and was deeply impressed by the talent that the young composer possessed, leading Haydn to invite the composer to study with him in Vienna. Currently considered the father of symphony and the pioneer of classical music, it was a grand opportunity for Beethoven to study under his tutelage. Their personalities, on the other hand, clashed heavily because of Beethoven’s fiery temper and Haydn’s calm nature. Beethoven was known to be very rebellious, combative, and irritable. Many speculate whether Beethoven had several mental health disorders that caused the bipolar nature in which he operated, his emotions frequently swinging back and forth between sinking depression and sharp anger. Regardless, this contrasted heavily with Haydn’s placid personality and teaching style. 

Said lessons took place in the course of Haydn’s phase of traveling, which forced Beethoven to seek lessons elsewhere in secret, so as not to offend his master, in Haydn’s absence. Their relationship was quite tumultuous, as Beethoven famously sought out Haydn’s advice on his third trio, which Haydn reviewed negatively, leaving a lasting impact on Beethoven’s pride. While the specifics of the criticism remain unknown, many speculate that it was due to its complexity and assume that the criticism was well-intentioned. Regardless, the prickly Beethoven was wounded by such a comment and published it anyway. 


This friction can be attributed to the fact that Haydn remained faithful to the established Classical tradition that he helped build, while Beethoven represented the evolution of the Classical, attempting to segue into the Romantic. This undoubtedly tainted Beethoven’s opinion of his old master, and he later claimed that he never learned anything from him, developing the opinion that Haydn was secretly jealous of him. 

Despite the conflict caused by the criticism and interpretive differences between the two, they remained on somewhat amiable terms later on, Beethoven dedicating his later piano concertos to his famous master. 

The piece that Haydn allegedly critiqued and advised Beethoven against publishing is called Piano Trio No.3 in C minor (Op.1, No.3). Ironically, what the younger composer considered the finest of his set, and what the more experienced composer said was lackluster, modern experts praise it as indeed being the most excellent among the three. The transitional late Classical-early Romantic piece was written in the early 1790s, but published in 1795 for Prince Lichnowsky, and was meant to be played by three instruments: the violin, the piano, and the cello. 

Nonetheless, as Beethoven metamorphosed both technically and musically during this period, his personal life remained in shambles. The abusive father, whom Beethoven loathed for the majority of his life, was declining both socially and physically. Due to his alcoholism that persisted after the death of his wife and a plethora of illnesses, Beethoven’s father and educational disciplinarian, Johann van Beethoven, passed away in Bonn in 1792. Already having had half of his father’s salary directed towards him to be able to support his family financially for several years at the time of Beethoven’s father’s demise, it can be assumed that the composer felt at least a slight sentiment of relief and confusion. Even though the death allowed Beethoven to emotionally move on from the abusive time of youth, transitioning into an independent and proper adulthood, the trauma would linger past this new era within his life, and undoubtedly affected the disposition and worldview of the blooming composer. Throughout his early twenties, he was described as a headstrong and temperamental man. His improvisational skills were bolstered and improved significantly, playing frequently in front of aristocrats and nobility, which further heightened his own notoriety. 


Although it wouldn’t prove to be a large problem at this point in his career, the young composer would slowly show indications of hearing loss in the mid 1790s, which he largely kept secret from the public, as it would be disastrous to his career if it came out. After all, it was almost a contradiction in and of itself to have a deaf musical composer. Not even middle-aged, his health problems would show hints of themselves through a high-pitched ringing in his ears. Nevertheless, foregoing the deterioration of his hearing, he was yet to reach his prime in his composition and technique. 


Beethoven’s Romantic Era 

Piano Sonata No.14: Moonlight Sonata


	The early 19th century was the start of the composer’s Romantic era, in both personal and compositional regard. It was frequently called his Heroic period. The works prior to this period were categorized as more classical, as the music world had been dominated by his predecessors, like Mozart and Haydn, who had defined that genre. His previous pieces reflected that ideal, being cleaner and emotionally more restrictive. This is when Beethoven would segue into romanticism, and hints of his personal style would weave within his Heroic-era works. 

	Almost as famous as Beethoven himself is his music dedicated to his numerous lovers. Many of these pieces appeared during his romantic transition. At this point in his life, he was an instructor in Vienna to a young Countess named Giulietta Guicciardi, a pianist, whom he became infatuated with while spending time with her. 

Born from this enamoration, the thirty-year-old composer would dedicate one of his most famous works to her, Piano Sonata No.14, also known as the Moonlight Sonata — a staple in piano student repertoire. The first movement is a slow and haunting melody, while the second and third are described as more technically advanced, namely, the third being the most, as it demands precision, stamina, and speed from the pianist playing it. Beethoven had fallen head-over-heels for his student, who was around sixteen years old in 1801, and to whom he wrote passionate love letters. It is speculated in Thayer’s biography of Beethoven that Giulietta was inclined to accept his proposal, but was forbidden from doing so by her father due to his lack of wealth and status comparable to that of Giulietta’s. This led to Beethoven being swiftly rejected by the Guicciardis, and Giulietta being married off to another family, leaving the composer heartbroken in its wake. 

As Beethoven aged out of being a budding young pianist, he gained more experience in both his instruments and his compositions. As his hearing faded bit by bit, the composer produced a plethora of works, which included symphonies, concertos, and string quartets. With these works, his reputation as a respectable composer grew. While his notoriety became increasingly more positive with the output of pieces, he also became more sullen and temperamental due to the combination of his fruitless love life and his diminishing hearing. Many historical texts testify to his mental instability provoked by his inability to hear, which was vital to his profession and personal happiness, and his bad luck in romance certainly affected the composer deeply. 

Regardless of the outcome of Beethoven’s intense infatuation with the young Countess during his early 
thirties, the sonata that he dedicated to her remains a significant landmark in classical music to this day. Giucciardi would be one of many ladies that the composer would romantically pursue in search of a wife. Another famed lover of his was Therese Malfatti, for whom he wrote the piece “Fur Elise,” a worldwide piano classic nearly a decade after his proposal to the Countess Guicciardi. Malfatti was another student under Beethoven, whom he proposed and was rejected once more. The piece, Fur Elise, is debated to have been written incorrectly when the publication was released posthumously. There were many candidates to whom Elise might have been, but the primary theory is that instead of transcribing “Fur Therese”, “Fur Elise” was written. 

	Throughout, nearly ten noble ladies have been documented to have had the romantic interests of the composer expressed to them, almost all of them having ended without marriage. Beethoven would never marry nor have children of his own, which deeply wounded him, as he was known for being a romantic, despite his brooding disposition. Beethoven’s desire to be loved was evident within his letters; a ten-page letter, scattered with affectionate names, was found after his death, presumably for another noblewoman whom he loved. 
	
Although Beethoven’s pursuit of a lover remained inconclusive even to his death, the sonatas and excerpts he wrote for those he considered precious are relevant to this day and are testaments to his eternal affection and love. 


Beethoven’s Golden Age

Symphony No.3 in E-flat major, Op.55 “Eroica”


	As expected of a prolific composer, during his mid 40s, Beethoven continued to teach budding young musicians, as others had done for him in his youth. Although his teaching style was nowhere near as physically and verbally abusive as the one that his father adhered to, many testify that Beethoven’s lessons were reflective of his personality, both being demanding and harsh. Beethoven was said to be a perfectionist, and that expectation was also passed down to those who studied beneath him. Nonetheless, he continued teaching those whom he believed to possess a true gift for the instrument. 
Carl Czerny, a famous pianist who was under the composer’s tutelage for three years since he was ten years old, recalled his teacher’s training to be intense. While excellent technical ability was expected, Czerny claimed that his teacher frequently and sharply emphasized the emotional interpretation of the piece that they were working on. But Czerny would testify that even though his teacher’s pedagogical methods were harsh, and that he himself was temperamental and moody, the training was effective. Coincidentally, it was through Czerny that Beethoven was able to meet another future composer, Franz Liszt, who was no less than twelve years old at that time. Liszt became a prominent composer who would continue the romantic composition style that Beethoven pioneered. These composers whom Beethoven taught would further push out his music and solidify his immortal status. Evident throughout history, all of the Classical composers would seemingly know or know of one another. 

One of the few compositions that Beethoven amongst his favorites was his third symphony in E-flat major. Widely considered to be one of the first leading works classified as romantic in his repertoire, the symphony “Eroica”, like its name, marked a transition with sweeping melodies and intimate melodies in between, which revealed Beethoven’s deteriorating mental state, which he worked feverishly to conceal in the privacy of his own home. 

Beethoven’s later life resembles the lives of other great Classical and Romantic composers of his era. However, his life differed from others when he gradually ceased giving public performances and exhibitions of his music due to his diminished hearing. Up to this point in his life, he conducted and played music until it all became too much in his forties. His progressive loss came to be devastating, as he relied more frequently on conversation books to communicate with his students and his friends. As confessed in an unsent letter to his brothers, in a written work coined the Heiligenstadt Testament, Beethoven confides that he felt deeply depressed and hopeless as he progressively lost the sense most precious and vital to him. While the public deemed him arrogant and standoffish, he writes that he was forced to isolate himself because of his unfathomable despair, and how the public misunderstood his disposition as misanthropic. Beethoven professed in the unpublished letters of his utter anguish and humiliation at his deafness, which was an immense threat to his career. Furthermore, he claims that the distress had escalated to the point that he felt suicidal ideations, and that only his art sufficiently motivated him to continue his diminishing life. Continuously shown throughout his life, his art seemed to be the only source of comfort and solace that Beethoven routinely returned to upon suffering tragically and quietly. 


Legalities, Metal Rods, and Symphonies 

String Quartet No.14


By 1816, Beethoven was confirmed to be almost or entirely deaf, which impacted his compositional skills, evident in his music. His compositions were continuously pushed out without his hearing by utilizing various methods. Through decades of experience, he was able to imagine the melodies in his head. As he became more fervent and desperate to hear the glorious melodies he composed once more, he removed the legs from his piano and stuck sticks into his mouth. This helped him write more music, as the sound waves travelled up the extension and into the back of his oral cavity to guide the frequencies closer to the ear more directly. In typical hearing loss, the higher frequencies are the first to go, as it requires the ear to be more precise to perceive. Therefore, his writing preferences were altered, opting to write with lower frequencies and notes than higher ones, which he could no longer hear. Despite undergoing numerous medical treatments from different physicians and practitioners, Beethoven’s health continued to decline. 

In the course of his late forties, Beethoven came across legal trouble regarding his nine-year-old nephew and his sister-in-law. Following the death of his brother, Beethoven fought for the custody of his nephew from his brother’s widow, whom he loved and prioritized. In 1815, claiming Johanna, the widow, was an unfit parent. Even though the motivations behind his actions were justified as an act of concern, many historians believe that this was a desperate attempt to build a meaningful human connection with his nephew, which he sorely craved after he was forced to isolate himself, concealing his physical and mental illness. The composer was eventually awarded custody, despite wanting to reside with his mother. 

Perhaps due to his pitiful last resort to love and be loved by a human being, Beethoven was excessive in his protection and control over the young Karl van Beethoven, driving him to attempt suicide at the age of nineteen in 1826. Shocked and distressed by his nephew’s actions, he tried to become less demanding and restrictive. 

At this point, the composer had lost his ability to hear altogether. Determined to write, pushing through distress, the majority of his greatest works, namely his fourteenth string quartet. Beethoven’s String Quartet No.14 was amongst his best and greatest works. It was also one of his more emotional works, reflecting the state of melancholic depression the composer was thrust into as he became deaf. Composed in C-sharp minor, it is described as introspective and obscure in tone. Other pieces were also written, like his Ninth Symphony, which he finished in 1824.  Beethoven’s diminishing state never stopped him from creating as much music as he desired to write. 


In 1827, shortly after the attempted suicide of his precious nephew, Beethoven was in the process of creating his tenth symphony. But he would never end up finishing it. Riddled with various conditions, provoked by alcohol consumption, stress, and lead poisoning, Ludwig van Beethoven passed away on the twenty-sixth of March that year. He was only fifty-six years old at the time of his agonizing demise. 

Three days after the composer breathed his last breath, a massive ceremonial funeral was held in his honor. Having earned the respect and admiration of those far and close to him, many of his former pupils and admirers, such as Franz Schubert, another famous composer, and family members, attended the massive procession with tens of thousands of mourners to honor the late composer. 


Conclusion 


	In the end, the late Classical and early Romantic composer, Ludwig van Beethoven, died with what he spent the majority of his life enamored with: music. Despite living through a traumatic childhood, a tumultuous adolescence, and a lonely old age, trapped in the silence where music usually was present, the composer was one of the greatest composers who ever lived. As frequently shown and proved over and over, his determination to create beautiful works of art for us to enjoy was the driving factor of his life. As humble as his name appeared to be in terms of origin, it fully cemented itself in humanity's memories regarding music. Even as disability threatened to strip away all that was dear to him, he would not let it steal the core of his being: his love for music.

Solis & Luna Arts is a club run at Bergen County Academies that believes in the power of healing through music, art, and dance. We have been operating for almost two months now. In this time, we have welcomed new members, perfected our performances, and planned new events. Things have gone quite smoothly, although we have certainly encountered our fair share of challenges.

The first big challenge we faced was developing and organizing our team. We had no shortage of potential members as students from various schools expressed their interest. However, it was up to club co-founders, Chloe Cho, Juni Myung, and Madhav Dua, to help each member find their place in the club. Members were sorted based on their artistic abilities into teams focusing on music, art, and even dance. Other members applied for leadership positions, which require management and communication skills. At a recent weekly meeting, club VP Juni Myung announced this year’s leadership board.

Even before our team was fully organized, our members were already preparing for upcoming events. The Art Team hit the ground running by developing a design for our club banner at our second meeting. In the time since, the team has perfected this design, and they cannot wait to display it at our events. Our Music Team has been hard at work, practicing a variety of pieces on the piano, cello, and more. Although the Dance Team has also gained a lot of interest, some time remains before they will actually perform. These three teams have been working on many different projects, yet one thing unites them all: their excitement for our events!

This weekend, Solis & Luna Arts will perform at St. Joseph’s Autism Center. Our meeting room has been filled with both anxiety and excitement over this concert. Obviously, our performers will be in attendance, but the Writing staff will also be sure to attend and document Solis & Luna Art’s experiences. If you would like to get a sense of what we have been up to, be sure to stop by this Saturday at 9:30!

Solis and Luna’s music team has prepared a total of 7 pieces for the event, listed below: “Can’t Help Falling in Love” by Elvis Presley performed by Danielle Shi, Maggie Richards, and Chloe Cho . “The Swan” by Saint Saëns performed by Madison Darnaby and Chloe Cho “Five Pieces for Two Violins and Piano” by Shostakovich performed by Chloe Cho and David Kim “My Way” by Frank Sinatraa performed by Aiden Hong, Leane Kwon, and Chloe Cho Violin Duo by Reger performed by Yumi Park and Janice Lee “What a Wonderful World” by Louis Armstrong performed by Chloe Cho and Matthew Lee “The Elephant” by Saint Saëns performed by Maggie Richards

The music team practices each of these pieces every Wednesday, bringing their own instruments and sheet music. Moreover, the music team have also met up with each other on their own time to play their best for the New Bridge Medical Center residents. After the success of their first concert, the music team hopes to continue their success by having a flawless performance in the New Bridge Medical Center.

On the other hand, the art team has been hard at work creating a banner for the club to hang up during the performance. Since the Latin words “Solis” and “Luna” translate into “sun” and “moon” respectively, the art team decided that the banner should resemble the sunrise and the night sky. The bottom half of “Solis” depicts the ocean, while the top half represents the yellow sky illuminated by the sun. “Luna” has been coloured in to show the night sky, filled by stars and the crescent moon. 

In conclusion, the members of Solis and Luna have been preparing really hard for this event and all the members are excited and hoping their second event goes well.

Our Essex County chapter recently collaborated with Keys 2 Success to put together a fun-filled night of music and camaraderie. Organized by Essex County Director Vivian Zhang, who has also been a long-time volunteer at Keys 2 Success, the event took place at Cafe Luna, a cozy local cafe in New Providence, New Jersey. The long-sought-after performance collaboration has finally happened after our director Chloey met with the director of Keys 2 Success Ms. Jee-Hoon Krska last spring. The program featured singing, piano solos from Keys 2 Success students, and lastly a rendition of Saint-Saëns’ Carnival of the Animals for the Keys 2 Success piano students and our Solis and Luna Arts members. In addition to a successful concert, we also enjoyed delicious homemade food and made many new friends with the Keys 2 Success volunteers, students, and supporters who come from all different backgrounds. The concert showcased music’s ability to transcend barriers and bring people together, and it also displayed the musical talents of all the performers!

In its first month of operation, Solis & Luna has already been featured in Bergen County Academies’ school newsletter, The Academy Chronicle! Take a look at what they had to say about us: 

Solis & Luna Arts (SLA) is a brand-new club at BCA which combines students’ passion for the arts with a desire to serve the community. SLA offers music, art, and dance therapies to various communities including veterans and senior citizens. 

On September 5th, two BCA sophomores, Chloe Cho and Juni Myung, founded this club after a conversation about their prior experiences performing. “For example, my grandpa is a veteran, and I sometimes play music for him and his veteran friends, which serves as music therapy. I used my music to help decrease anxiety, depression, and more,” Chloe said.

Upon discussing, the two students realized that not many people are aware of the value of these forms of therapy. “We wanted to make a club and even a nonprofit to raise awareness. Our classmates could get involved and see the benefits for themselves.”

However, Chloe realized that making a new club was not as simple as she first expected. “[Juni and I] submitted our club proposal to try and make it an official Wednesday club. But when I submitted, Mrs. Kouefati asked if we could combine with the Music History club due to limited spots. Luckily, we ended up not having to merge. If we did, the club would have been pretty unproductive as the other club had very different goals.”

SLA hit the ground running after gaining its status as an official club. They are about to celebrate the launch of their new website which will feature blog posts, updates, and more.

Unfortunately for the club, there are still some roadblocks ahead. Chloe and Juni are in the middle of registering as an official non-profit organization, a lengthy and arduous process. “[Registering] will help Solis & Luna in many ways. We can give our members community service hours and some other special privileges, but it is very difficult,” Chloe said.

It is clear that SLA is one of BCA’s most ambitious new clubs. Stay up to date with Solis & Luna Arts by checking out their soon-to-be-released website!
